Touch the roof of your mouth with your tongue, then release the air quickly. Keep your vocal cords quiet for this sound. To make the next sound, touch the back of your mouth with your tongue and release the air. For the last sound, round your lips and push continuous air smoothly over your tongue.

## Spelling rules

In most native English words, the group ch sounds like /tʃ/, as in (rich) /rɪtʃ/. In words from Greek, the group sounds like /k/, as in (echo) /ɛk.oʊ/. In words borrowed from modern French, it sounds like /ʃ/, as in (chef) /ʃɛf/.

## Common mistakes

Do not soften the primary sound into a continuous hiss. Stop the air completely before releasing it with a quick pop. Since this is your own language, you usually pick the correct sound naturally without difficulty.
articles.summary: Letter name: ch. Example: chair.

articles.title: ch
articles.body:
## Sound of ch

The letters ch are named /k/. Their main sound is the sound /tʃ/, heard in the word (chin) /tʃɪn/, which means the bottom part of your face. These letters make three different sounds in English.

## How to say ch

For the first sound, press your tongue tip behind your upper teeth. Stop the breath, then release it with a quick puff. For the second sound, lift the back of your tongue against the roof of your mouth and release a clean burst of air. For the third sound, round your lips slightly and blow air steadily over your tongue. Your throat does not buzz for any of them. Put a hand on your throat to check.

## Spelling of ch

In native English words, these letters usually sound like the sound /tʃ/, as in (rich) /rɪtʃ/. In words borrowed from Greek, they make the sound /k/, as in (echo) /ɛk.oʊ/ or (ache) /eɪk/. In words borrowed from French, they make the sound /ʃ/, as in (chef) /ʃɛf/ and (chic) /ʃiːk/.

## Common mistakes with ch

Do not let your throat buzz when you make these sounds. A common error is blending the sounds into a smooth glide instead of stopping the air. Make sure you stop the air completely before releasing the puff.
articles.summary: Letter name: ch. Example: chorus.

articles.title: ch
articles.body:
## Sounds of ch

The letters ch are called /ʃ/. Their primary sound is heard in the word (chin) /tʃɪn/, which means the chin. These letters can produce four different sounds across English words.

## How to say ch

For the first sound, press your tongue tip behind your upper teeth, then release air sharply. For the second sound, lift the back of your tongue against the soft roof of your mouth and release air. For the third sound, push your lips forward into a circle and blow air gently over your tongue. For the last variant, keep your mouth still because you make no sound. Touch your throat to feel that your voice stays quiet.

## Spelling patterns

In native English words, these letters usually make the sound /tʃ/, as in (rich) /rɪtʃ/. In words borrowed from Greek, they make the sound /k/, as in (chemist) /kɛm.ɪst/ and (echo) /ɛk.oʊ/. In modern borrowings from French, they make the sound /ʃ/, as in (chef) /ʃɛf/ and (machine) /mə.ʃin/. In a few rare borrowings, the letters are not pronounced, as in (yacht) /jɑt/.

## Common mistakes

You may mix up the three main sounds of these letters. Do not say the sound /ʃ/ when a word needs the sharp sound /tʃ/. Do not use the sound /k/ in native words. Pay close attention to word origins to choose the correct sound.
articles.summary: Letter name: ch. Example: machine.

articles.title: ph
articles.body:
## Sound of ph

The letters ph make the sound /f/. You hear this sound in the word (photo) /foʊ.toʊ/, which means a picture taken with a camera. This letter combination makes two different sounds in English words. Most words use only the first sound.

## How to say ph

To make the first sound, place your upper teeth on your lower lip. Blow air gently through the gap without using your voice. To make the second sound, keep your mouth in the same position. Blow air through the gap and turn your voice on. Put a hand on your throat to feel the buzz.

## Spelling of ph

The letters ph usually make the sound /f/ in words from Greek, such as (phone) /foʊn/ and (dolphin) /dɑl.fɪn/. In the name (Stephen) /sti.vən/, these letters make the sound /v/ instead.

## Common mistakes

Do not pronounce the letters separately as two sounds. Never say the sound in pet followed by the sound in hat. Keep your upper teeth on your lower lip, and push the air smoothly through your mouth.
articles.summary: Letter name: ph. Example: phone.

articles.title: ng
articles.body:
## Sound of ng

The letters ng are called the sound /ŋ/. Their main sound is the sound /ŋ/, as in (sing) /sɪŋ/. To (sing) /sɪŋ/ means to make music with your voice. This letter group makes two sounds in English words.

## How to say ng

To make the first sound, lift the back of your tongue against the soft roof of your mouth. Let air flow out through your nose while your voice hums. Touch your throat to feel the strong vibration. For the second sound, make that same humming nose sound, then finish with a quick puff of voice from your throat.

## Spelling patterns of ng

At the end of a word, you say the sound /ŋ/, like in (ring) /rɪŋ/. Inside the middle of a root word before a vowel, you pronounce the sound /ŋɡ/, like in (finger) /fɪŋ.ɡər/.

## Comparing ng

Learners often add a hard click at the end of simple words. Do not let your tongue drop suddenly. Keep the back of your tongue touching the roof until your voice stops completely. Also, do not replace this sound with a simple sound made at your front teeth.
articles.summary: Letter name: ng. Example: sing.

articles.title: -tion
articles.body:
## The ending tion

The ending tion is spoken as /ʃən/. It sounds like the end of the word (action) /æk.ʃən/, which means an act or movement. This ending makes two different sounds in English words.

## How to say tion

For the first sound, round your lips slightly. Push air through the gap without your voice, then relax into a weak ending. For the second sound, press the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth. Release the air suddenly with a soft hiss before the weak ending. Hold your hand against your throat to feel that your voice stays off during both starts.

## Spelling rules for tion

In most words, this ending is unstressed and makes the sound /ʃən/, as heard in (nation) /neɪ.ʃən/. When the letters come right after the letter s, they make the sound /tʃən/, as heard in (question) /kwes.tʃən/.

## Common mistakes with tion

Do not read the letters as separate sounds like tee on. Always use a soft rushing sound or a quick stop sound at the start. Do not say a clear vowel like on at the end. Keep the final vowel very short and weak, so it does not sound like the full vowel in off.
articles.summary: Letter name: -tion. Example: nation.

articles.title: -eigh
articles.body:
## Sound of -eigh

The letters eigh sound like /eɪ/. Their main sound is heard in the word (weigh) /weɪ/, which means to measure how heavy something is. This spelling has two different sounds in English. You never pronounce the individual letters separately.

## How to say -eigh

To make the first sound, spread your lips and raise the front of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Glide smoothly upward toward a narrower vowel. For the second sound, open your jaw wider, then move your tongue upward. Put a hand on your throat to feel your voice buzz throughout both sounds.

## Spelling of -eigh

Most words with this spelling use the sound /eɪ/. You hear this pattern in (sleigh) /sleɪ/. In a few words, this spelling makes the sound /aɪ/. You hear this pattern in (height) /haɪt/.

## Mistakes with -eigh

Do not try to speak the letters g and h. They are silent here. Do not stop after the first part of the glide. Make sure your tongue moves upward until the vowel finishes cleanly.
articles.summary: Letter name: -eigh. Example: eight.

articles.title: -ough
articles.body:
## The group ough

The letters ough do not have an official name. The main sound of the letters ough is heard in the word (through) /θruː/, which means moving from one side to the other. This spelling pattern has four different sounds.

## Making the sounds

For the first sound, push your lips into a tight circle and make a long tone. For the second sound, round your lips loosely and glide them tighter. For the third sound, open your mouth wide and make a long, open tone. For the last sound, keep your mouth relaxed, and touch your upper teeth with your lower lip to blow air.

## Reading the letters

In some base words, the letters ough sound like /uː/. In words like (though) /ðoʊ/, the letters ough sound like /oʊ/. When the letter t follows, the letters ough make the open sound /ɔː/, as in (thought) /θɔːt/. In words like (rough) /rʌf/, the letters ough sound like /ʌf/.

## Common mistakes

Do not read these letters the same way in every word. In words with the /f/ sound, do not drop the blowing air. Remember to check whether the letters make a vowel or end with an f sound.
articles.summary: Letter name: -ough. Example: through.

articles.title: -ough
articles.body:
## The group ough

The letters ough are called the sound /oʊ/. Their main sound is the sound /oʊ/, as in (though) /ðoʊ/, which means although. This letter group makes four different sounds in common everyday speech.

## How to say it

For the first sound, round your lips and move them inward into a smaller circle. For the second sound, push your lips forward into a tight ring. For the third sound, open your jaw wide and pull your tongue back. For the fourth sound, open your mouth slightly and touch your lower lip to your upper teeth.

## When to use it

The letters ough make the sound /oʊ/ in (dough) /doʊ/. They make the sound /uː/ in (through) /θruː/. They make the long sound /ɔː/ before t in (thought) /θɔːt/. They make the sound /ʌf/ with an f-sound in (rough) /rʌf/.

## Common mistakes

Do not speak every word with this pattern the same way. Check each word in a dictionary because the letters do not follow one single rule.
articles.summary: Letter name: -ough. Example: though.

articles.title: -ough
articles.body:
## The group ough

The letters ough make the sound /ɔː/ in (bought) /bɔːt/. This word means you paid money for something. The group can make four different sounds.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide and make a circle with your lips for the first sound. For the next sound, begin with a round mouth and pull your lips together. For the third sound, push your lips forward into a small tight ring. For the last sound, keep your mouth open, then touch your lower lip to your upper teeth with blowing air. Place your fingers on your throat to feel voice for the vowels.

## Reading the spelling

Before t in past words, the group makes the sound /ɔː/ as in (thought) /θɔːt/. At the end of some words, it makes the sound /oʊ/ as in (though) /ðoʊ/. It makes the long sound /uː/ in (through) /θruː/. In other words, it sounds like /ʌf/ as in (rough) /rʌf/.

## Common mistakes

Do not speak every letter in this group. The letters g and h are often completely silent. Remember that the vowel changes between words, so you must learn each word alone.
articles.summary: Letter name: -ough. Example: thought.

articles.title: ea in seară (evening)
articles.body:
## The sound ea

The letters ea sound like /e̯a/. Their main sound appears in (seară) /ˈse̯a.rə/, which means evening. These letters make only one sound in Romanian. You say them smoothly together in one single push of air.

## How to say ea

Start with your lips spread slightly as if smiling. Place your tongue high and forward in your mouth. Quickly drop your jaw and open your mouth wide. Let your tongue fall low and flat. Touch your throat with your hand to feel the steady vibration of your voice.

## Spelling of ea

The letters ea make the sound /e̯a/ in stressed parts of a word. You can hear this glide in (cafea) /kaˈfe̯a/. The two letters always stay in the exact same beat.

## Mistakes to avoid

Do not turn these letters into two separate beats like the vowels in react. Do not pronounce them as the long vowel in tea. Glide smoothly from the first sound to the second without stopping.
articles.summary: The diphthong ea is found in the Romanian word seară.

articles.title: oa in noapte (night)
articles.body:
## The group oa

The letters oa make the sound /o̯a/. Hear this sound in the word (oameni) /ˈno̯ap.te/, which means night. This letter combination makes one single gliding sound in Romanian.

## Pronouncing oa

Round your lips slightly for a brief start. Then open your mouth wide and relax your lips completely. Let your voice flow continuously from the back to the front. You can feel your jaw drop as the sound finishes.

## Spelling rules

The letters oa make the sound /o̯a/ in stressed syllables, as in (noapte) /ˈno̯ap.te/. They also make the sound /o̯a/ in the word (soare) /ˈso̯a.re/.

## Common mistakes

Do not pronounce each letter as two separate vowels like in boa. Do not say the vowel in boat. Glide smoothly from a quick round vowel into a clear open sound.
articles.summary: The diphthong oa is found in the Romanian word noapte.

articles.title: ia in iarnă (winter)
articles.body:
## The group ia

The letters ia sound like the name /ja/. Their main sound appears in (iarnă) /ˈjar.nə/, which means winter. This letter group makes two different sounds.

## Pronouncing the group

For the first sound, push your tongue high and forward. Then drop your jaw quickly to an open vowel. Your voice vibrates throughout the whole motion. For the second sound, make a full clear ee vowel first. Then open your mouth completely for a separate ah sound. Feel your throat buzz constantly with your fingers.

## Reading the spelling

When the two letters sit in the same syllable, they make the quick gliding sound /ja/, as in (băiat) /bəˈjat/. When the vowels split across two syllables, pronounce two distinct beats with the sound /i.a/, as in (pian) /piˈan/.

## Avoiding mistakes

Do not turn the gliding pair into two slow vowels. In words with one syllable, say it quickly like the sound in yard. Also, avoid changing the open vowel to the sound in cat. Keep the second vowel wide and open like the sound in father.
articles.summary: The diphthong ia is found in the Romanian word iarnă.

articles.title: ie in ieri (yesterday)
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter group ie sounds like /je/. You hear this sound in (ieri) /jerʲ/, which means yesterday. This letter pair makes one sound.

## How to say it

Raise the middle of your tongue high toward the roof of your mouth. Keep your lips wide and spread. Glide swiftly into an open mouth while lowering your tongue. Your vocal cords vibrate all the time. Place a hand on your throat to feel the steady vibration.

## Spelling rules

The group ie makes the sound /je/ in most positions. You hear it in words like (fier) /fjer/.

## Common mistakes

Do not turn this letter pair into two separate vowels. English words like alien or spaniel have a quick gliding sound. Keep both parts in one single breath. Never pause between the two letters.
articles.summary: The diphthong ie is found in the Romanian word ieri.

articles.title: io in iod (iodine)
articles.body:
## The sound io

The letters io sound like the sequence /jo/. Their main sound is heard in the word (iod) /jod/, which means iodine. These letters have two different pronunciations in Romanian speech.

## Mouth shape

First glide quickly from a tight tongue position to a circle. Raise your tongue high near the roof of your mouth, then move into an o shape while making sound. For the other variant, make two separate sounds. Say a clear ee, then shape your lips into a small circle for o. Touch your throat to feel your voice buzz throughout both sounds.

## Spelling rules

The letters io usually merge into the quick sound /jo/, as in (ghiozdan) /ɡjozˈdan/. In foreign loans and words with prefixes, the two vowels split across two syllables, making the sound /i.o/. You hear this separate rhythm in (biologie) /bi.o.loˈd͡ʒi.e/ and (avion) /a.viˈon/.

## Common mistakes

Do not replace the first sound with a long vowel from words like see. Keep the glide fast and smooth, like the y in yoke. Do not blend the letters when they belong to separate beats. Say both parts distinctly.
articles.summary: The diphthong io is found in the Romanian word iod.

articles.title: iu in iubit (beloved)
articles.body:
## The sound of iu

The letters iu are called the sound /ju/. They make the sound /ju/ in (iubit) /juˈbit/, which means beloved. These two letters can make two different sound patterns.

## How to say iu

For the first sound, lift your tongue high and forward, then round your lips tightly. Your voice flows smoothly from a quick glide into the vowel. For the second sound, make two separate beats. Hold your tongue high and flat for the first beat. Then push your lips forward into a circle for the second beat. Place a hand on your throat to feel continuous vibration.

## Spelling rules for iu

When the two letters sit in one single syllable, they make the sound /ju/, as in (iute) /ˈju.te/. When each letter sits in its own syllable, you hear two clear vowels as the sound /i.u/, as in (știu) /ʃti.u/. This split also happens across syllables in (triumf) /triˈumf/.

## Common mistakes with iu

Do not swallow the first vowel when the pair splits into two beats. In words with two syllables, do not rush through the letters like the quick glide in you. Say each vowel fully, giving each its own clear pulse of voice.
articles.summary: The diphthong iu is found in the Romanian word iubit.

articles.title: ua in ziua (the day)
articles.body:
## The group ua

The letters ua make the sound /wa/. You hear this in the word (ziua) /ˈzi.wa/, which means the day. This letter pair has one sound.

## Making the sound

First round your lips into a tight circle, like making a quick English sound w. Then open your lips wide and drop your jaw to make the sound a. Your vocal cords vibrate during the whole movement. Put your hand on your throat to feel the buzzing.

## Spelling rules

The letters ua always make the sound /wa/ when they appear together in the same syllable. You can hear this in (roua) /ˈro.wa/.

## Common mistakes

Do not separate the two letters into two full, slow vowels like oo followed by ah. Glide quickly from the lip circle to the open vowel, exactly as in the English word water.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong ua as found in the word ziua.

articles.title: ue in înșeuează (saddles)
articles.body:
## The letters ue

The letters ue sound like /we/. Their main sound is heard in (înșeuează) /ɨn.ʃe.we̯aˈza/, which means saddles a horse. This combination makes one sound.

## How to say it

Make a small tight circle with your lips. Glide smoothly into an open smile. Vibrate your vocal cords with your voice throughout the glide. You can feel your throat buzz with your fingers.

## Spelling rules

These two letters sound like the sound /we̯/ within a single syllable, as in (leului) /ˈlew.luj/.

## Common mistakes

Do not turn this glide into two slow vowels. Move quickly like the start of wet. Keep your lips tight at first.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong ue as found in the word înșeuează.

articles.title: ai in mai (May / more)
articles.body:
## The letter group ai

The letters ai are spoken as the sound /aj/. They make the main sound in the word (mai) /maj/, which means more or May. This letter group has two spoken forms in Romanian.

## How to say it

For the first sound, open your mouth wide. Glide your tongue up towards the roof of your mouth. Your lips stay relaxed. For the other sound, open your mouth wide first. Then lift your tongue high and smile to make a separate second vowel. Touch your throat to feel your voice buzz throughout.

## When to use each

The letters ai usually blend into one syllable as the sound /aj/, like in (haină) /ˈhaj.nə/. When separated across two syllables, they sound as two distinct vowels with the sound /a.i/, as heard in (aurit) /a.uˈrit/.

## Common mistakes

Do not make this sound like the vowel in the English word rain. The Romanian sound is much more open, exactly like the vowel sound in the English word my. Move smoothly from an open vowel to a quick glide without adding extra puff of air.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong ai as found in the word mai.

articles.title: ei in trei (three)
articles.body:
## The sound ei

The letters ei sound like the sound /ej/. You hear this in the word (trei) /trej/, which means three. This letter combination makes two different sounds in Romanian words.

## Mouth movements

For the first sound, start with your mouth half open and your tongue forward. Glide quickly into a short, high tongue position. For the second sound, make the first vowel clearly, and then make a full second vowel. You can feel your voice box vibrate continuously throughout both sounds.

## Reading the letters

In one syllable, the letters make the sound /ej/, as in (lei) /lej/. Across two syllables, each letter has its own beat, making the sound /e.i/. You hear this split sound in the word (atei) /aˈte.i/.

## Common mistakes

Do not make the long English sound heard in the word say. Keep the first part crisp, and glide rapidly. When the vowels sit in separate syllables, do not blend them together into one syllable.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong ei as found in the word trei.

articles.title: oi in doi (two)
articles.body:
## The sound of oi

The letters oi sound like the sound /oj/. You hear them in the word (doi) /doj/, which means two. This pair makes only one sound in Romanian.

## How to say oi

Round your lips tightly and pull your tongue back. Start making a clear vowel sound. Then quickly glide your tongue up and forward toward your upper teeth. Spread your lips slightly at the end. Your voice box vibrates all the time. Place a hand on your throat to feel the steady vibration throughout the sound.

## Spelling rules for oi

The letters oi make the sound /oj/ in all positions. You hear it at the end of the word (foi) /foj/. It also appears with the exact same sound in the middle of words.

## Mistakes with oi

You may stretch this pair into two separate vowels. Do not say two syllables as in the English word fluid. The letters oi glide together quickly in one single push of air. They sound very close to the end of the English word boy.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong oi as found in the word doi.

articles.title: ui in pui (chicken / you put)
articles.body:
## The sound ui

The letters ui sound as /uj/. Their main sound appears in (pui) /puj/, which means chicken or youth. This letter pair has two sounds in Romanian.

## Mouth movements

For the first sound, round your lips tightly. Glide quickly to a sharp sound while spreading your lips wide. For the second sound, make two distinct beats. First push your lips forward into a small circle. Then shift your tongue high and forward for a clear separate sound. Touch your throat to feel steady voicing throughout.

## Spelling rules

The letters ui make the single gliding sound /uj/ within one syllable, as in (puiul) /ˈpu.jul/. They split into two separate vowel beats /u.i/ across syllables, as heard in (ruină) /ruˈi.nə/ and (construit) /kon.struˈit/.

## Common mistakes

Do not turn this pair into the single vowel of English fruit or juice. You must pronounce both elements clearly. In a single syllable, slide smoothly from the first sound to the second without stopping. Across two syllables, keep each vowel fully independent and never drop either sound.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong ui as found in the word pui.

articles.title: au in sau (or)
articles.body:
## Sound of au

The letters au make the sound /aw/. You hear this sound in (sau) /saw/, which means or. This letter group makes only one sound.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide and keep your tongue low and flat. Then glide smoothly toward a tight circle with your lips. Your tongue pulls back slightly. Your vocal cords vibrate throughout the glide. Touch your throat to feel continuous vibration from start to finish.

## Spelling rules

The letters au make the sound /aw/ when spoken together in one syllable. You can hear this sound in (daur) /dawr/.

## Common mistakes

You might pronounce this sound like the vowel sound in the English word now. In Romanian, keep the first part bright and open before you glide. Do not start with a flat tongue resting in the middle of your mouth.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong au as found in the word sau.

articles.title: eu in greu (heavy / hard)
articles.body:
## The Sound

The sequence **eu** typically forms a falling diphthong pronounced `/ew/`, gliding smoothly from a mid-front vowel to a rounded semivowel. It resembles the vowel glide in the Portuguese word *meu* or a rapid transition from English *bed* to *book*. Note that in the singular subject pronoun **eu** ('I'), standard Romanian adds a prothetic glide, pronouncing it as `/jew/`.

## How to Say It

Start with your lips unrounded and your tongue positioned mid-front, exactly as you would pronounce the Romanian vowel `[e]`. Without breaking the airflow, glide your lips smoothly into a tight, rounded shape while pulling the tongue back toward `[w]`. Keep both parts within the same syllable, allowing the first vowel to take the primary acoustic stress.

## Spelling Patterns

This letter pair is written as lowercase **eu** and capitalized as **Eu** at the beginning of sentences. It frequently appears at the end of adjectives, adverbs, and nouns, such as in **greu** ('heavy') or **muzeu** ('museum'). In most lexical items it forms a true diphthong in a single syllable, though in neologisms with Greek or Romance roots it may sometimes split into hiatus.

## Accent and Variations

Do not confuse the falling diphthong `/ew/` found in **greu** or **mereu** with the pronoun **eu**, which standard orthoepy transcribes with an initial glide as `/jew/`. Foreign learners often make the mistake of separating the two letters into two distinct syllables like *e-u*. Ensure you glide the sounds together into one coherent unit unless an explicit grammatical hiatus occurs.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong eu as found in the word greu.

articles.title: eai in vedeai (you used to see)
articles.body:
## The sound of eai

The letters eai sound like /e̯aj/. You hear this group in the word (vedeai) /veˈde̯aj/, which means you were seeing. These letters make only one combined sound in Romanian. You say all three vowels together in one single breath.

## Mouth movements

Start with your tongue mid high and glide quickly. Open your mouth wide for the main vowel sound. Then raise your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Your lips stay spread throughout the glide. Your voice vibrates across the whole flow. Put your fingers on your throat to feel the steady vibration.

## When it appears

The letters eai appear in stressed syllables. They always make the sound /e̯aj/. You find them at the end of past tense verbs, like in (spuneai) /spuˈne̯aj/.

## Common mistakes

Do not split these letters into three separate syllables. English words like eye or aye start directly on an open vowel. Glide smoothly from a brief front vowel instead. Keep the entire sequence within one syllable.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong eai as found in the verb form vedeai.

articles.title: iai in tăiai (you were cutting)
articles.body:
## Sound of iai

The letters iai are spoken as the sound /jaj/. You hear this group in (tăiai) /təˈjaj/, which means you were cutting. This letter group makes only one combined sound in Romanian words. Listen to how smoothly the three letters blend together into one flowing unit.

## How to say iai

Lift your tongue high and forward near the roof of your mouth. Glide quickly down into a wide open mouth. Then glide your tongue high and forward again. Keep your vocal cords vibrating all the time. Feel the steady vibration by placing a hand on your throat.

## Spelling of iai

The letters iai make the sound /jaj/ in a single syllable. You hear this sound at the end of (apropiai) /a.pro.piˈjaj/. The group stays together as one flowing syllable in verb forms.

## Comparing iai

You might separate these letters into two distinct syllables. Do not pause between the letters. The whole sequence sounds like the word yay in English. Say it as one single continuous movement without any break.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong iai as found in the verb form tăiai.

articles.title: eau in beau (I drink / they drink)
articles.body:
## The group eau

The group eau is spoken as the sound /e̯aw/. You can hear it in the word (beau) /be̯aw/, which means I drink. This letter combination makes only one sound in Romanian. It glides through three vowel parts in a single breath.

## How to say eau

Start with your lips spread slightly. Drop your jaw quickly to open the mouth. Then round your lips into a small circle at the very end. Keep your voice turned on without stopping the airflow. Put a hand on your throat to feel continuous vibration throughout the glide.

## Spelling of eau

The letters eau appear together in a single syllable as the sound /e̯aw/. You see this group often at the end of past tense verbs. For example, it appears in the verb (vedeau) /veˈde̯aw/.

## Mistakes to avoid

Do not read this group as three separate vowels. Do not say it like the French word beau or the English sound in boat. Glide smoothly from an e sound through an open vowel to a quick w sound.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong eau as found in the verb form beau.

articles.title: iau in iau (I take / they take)
articles.body:
## The Sound of “iau”

The Romanian sequence **iau** represents a true triphthong pronounced as `[jaw]`. It starts with a brief palatal glide like the *y* in *yard*, shifts cleanly into an open, central *a*, and glides out into a rounded bilabial semivowel like the *w* in *cow*. Unlike in English where three vowels are often split across syllables, all three vowel elements here merge tightly into a single uninterrupted pulse.

## How to Pronounce “iau”

Start with your tongue high and forward as if saying a quick `[j]`. Immediately drop your jaw low to articulate a clear, resonant `[a]`, which carries the main stress. Without pausing the vocal cord vibration, round your lips and raise the back of your tongue toward the soft palate to glide out into a soft `[w]`.

## Spelling and Occurrence

This combination is written simply as **iau** in lowercase and **Iau** at the beginning of a sentence. It functions most famously as the monosyllabic verb form *iau* (meaning 'I take' or 'they take', from *a lua*). It also appears at the end of imperfect tense verbs such as *tăiau* ('they were cutting') or *beiau* ('they were drinking').

## Comparing and Common Errors

Learners commonly make the mistake of breaking this triphthong into two or three separate syllables, pronouncing it like *ee-ah-oo*. In Romanian, `[jaw]` must remain strictly monosyllabic and fluent, sliding seamlessly through the three qualities. Pay attention to keeping the middle vowel `[a]` full and open while treating the outer elements as light, rapid glides.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian diphthong iau as found in the verb form iau.

articles.title: ioa in creioane (pencils)
articles.body:
## The group ioa

The group ioa makes the complex sound /jo̯a/. You hear it in the word (creioane) /kreˈjo̯a.ne/, which means pencils. This group makes only one sound in Romanian. It glides through three vowels in one breath.

## How to say ioa

Start with your tongue high and front, as in yes. Pull your lips into an open ring for an o vowel. Open your mouth wide right away to finish on a clear a. Your voice runs smoothly through all three positions without stopping. Place your hand on your throat to feel continuous vibration.

## Spelling rules for ioa

The letters ioa appear inside stressed syllables. They sound like /jo̯a/ in the word (aripioară) /a.riˈpjo̯a.rə/. The three letters always stay together in the same beat.

## Common mistakes with ioa

Do not split this group into separate syllables. English words rarely combine these three sounds in one push. Connect the glide directly into the vowel as in the start of yard, but pass quickly through an o. Keep your tongue active and avoid pausing between the vowels.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the Romanian triphthong ioa as found in the noun creioane.

articles.title: ch in cherry (/tʃ/)
articles.body:
## Sounds of Ce and Ci

This letter pair is called /tʃe/, /tʃi/. It makes the main sound /tʃ/, as in (ceai) /tʃe/, which means request, petition. This spelling has two sounds in spoken Romanian.

## How to say it

For the main sound, press the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth. Release the air with a soft hiss. Your vocal cords do not vibrate. For the second sound, make this same release while raising the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Hold your hand against your throat to feel that your voice stays silent.

## Reading rules

Before the letters e or i, read the sound /tʃ/, as in (cine) /ˈtʃi.ne/. At the end of a word before a faint i, read the soft sound /tʃj/, as in (saci) /satʃʲ/.

## Useful contrasts

Do not pronounce this group like the hard k sound in cat. You must always say it like the soft sound in church. Keep the sound sharp and quick without adding a full vowel after it at the end of a word.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the digraph ch representing the sound /tʃ/ as in the word cherry.

articles.title: j in jam (/dʒ/)
articles.body:
## The sound

You call this group /dʒe/ or /dʒi/. Its primary pronunciation is the sound /d͡ʒ/, that is a voiced jam sound, heard in (gem) /ˈd͡ʒem/, meaning frost, severe cold. It produces two distinct sounds.

## How to say it

Touch the roof of your mouth with your tongue tip. Push air through firmly while your vocal cords vibrate, and release. For the second sound, make this same release while flattening your tongue against the roof. Feel your neck buzz with your fingers.

## Reading the letters

Before the vowels e or i, read the sound /d͡ʒ/, that is a full voiced jam sound. You hear this sound in (ger) /d͡ʒer/. At the end of a word after this group, make the sound /d͡ʒʲ/, that is a softened voiced sound. This occurs in (dragi) /drad͡ʒʲ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not turn this letter group into the hard sound in get. Speak it gently as in judge. At the end of a word, do not add a full vowel like English energy. Cut the airflow instantly.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the letter j representing the sound /dʒ/ as in the word jam.

articles.title: k in key (/k/)
articles.body:
## Sounds of Che and Chi

The letter group is called /ke/, /ki/. Its main sound is heard in (chelner) /kʲe̯e/, which means key. This spelling represents two sound variants in Romanian.

## How to Say It

For the first sound, press the middle of your tongue against the hard roof of your mouth. Release the air suddenly without any voice. For the second variant, make the same crisp stop at the end of a word, but add a soft breath. Hold your palm near your lips to feel that tiny puff of air.

## Spelling Rules

Before e or i, the letters make the sound /kʲ/, that is a soft k before a vowel. You hear this in (cheie) /ˈkʲe.je/. At the very end of a word, the group makes the sound /kʲ/, that is a soft k whisper. You can hear it in (vechi) /vekʲ/.

## Common Mistakes

Do not pronounce this group like the ch in cheese. It is always a hard, soft k sound, like the k in kitchen. Keep your tongue high against the roof of your mouth. Do not add an English w sound after it.
articles.summary: This item illustrates the letter k representing the sound /k/ as in the word key.

articles.title: g in get / give (/g/)
articles.body:
## The sound

These letters are called /ge/, /gi/. They make the sound /ɡʲ/, as in the word (gheață) /ˈɡe̯at͡sə/, which means ice. This group makes only one sound in Romanian.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Keep the middle of your tongue high and close to the roof. Release the air suddenly with your voice. Touch your throat to feel your vocal cords buzz.

## Spelling rules

The letters ghe or ghi always make the sound /ɡʲ/. You hear this sound before e or i, as in the word (ghid) /ɡid/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the sound like the soft sound in the English word gem. It is a hard sound, like the g in geese. Always keep the sound fully voiced and sharp.
articles.summary: The letter g represents the voiced velar plosive sound /g/ as in the words get and give.

articles.title: ea
articles.body:
## Sound of ea

The letters ea have no single name. Their main sound is the long vowel /iː/, as heard in (eat) /iːt/, which means to take food. Together these letters make three distinct vowel sounds across English words.

## How to say ea

For the first sound, spread your lips wide and raise your tongue high near the roof. For the second sound, relax your lips and open your mouth a little wider. For the third sound, slide smoothly from a mid vowel into a high front vowel. Touch your throat to feel your voice buzz continuously for each one.

## Spelling of ea

Most commonly, these letters make the long sound /iː/, as in (meat) /miːt/. Before certain consonants like d, th, or l, they often make the short sound /ɛ/, as in (bread) /brɛd/. In a few special words, they sound like /eɪ/, as in (great) /ɡreɪt/.

## Comparing ea

Learners often confuse the short vowel with the long vowel. Do not make the vowel too long in every word with these letters. Keep the mouth slightly open and steady instead of stretching your smile. Pay close attention to exceptions where the letters sound like a gliding vowel.
articles.summary: This is the letter L317 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: ee
articles.body:
## Sound of the letters

The letters ee sound like the long vowel /iː/. Their standard sound is the sound in (tree) /triː/, which means a tall plant with wood and leaves. These two letters have two sounds in total. Most words use the long sound, but some common words use a shorter sound instead.

## How to say it

For the first sound, spread your lips wide into a smile. Raise the front of your tongue close to the top of your mouth. For the second sound, relax your tongue slightly down and toward the center. Keep your lips relaxed rather than spread wide. Feel your vocal cords vibrate with your hand on your throat for both sounds.

## Spelling rules

In most regular words, these letters produce the long sound /iː/, as in (see) /siː/. They also make that same sound in the middle of a word, as in (feed) /fiːd/. In a few special words, these letters produce the shorter sound /ɪ/, as in (been) /bɪn/.

## Common mistakes

Do not make the long sound too short, like the vowel in sit. Remember to spread your lips into a clear smile and stretch the sound. When you say the shorter vowel, do not tense your mouth into a full smile. Relax your lips and tongue so the vowel does not sound like seat.
articles.summary: This is the letter L318 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: ai
articles.body:
## The letters ai

The letters ai make the sound /eɪ/. You hear this main sound in (rain) /reɪn/, which means water that falls from clouds. This letter group makes three different sounds in English.

## Mouth movements

For the first sound, open your mouth slightly and spread your lips wide. Move your jaw upward as your tongue glides toward your upper teeth. For the next sound, drop your jaw slightly and keep your tongue flat. For the last sound, relax your tongue and lips completely in the middle of your mouth. Your vocal cords vibrate for each sound.

## Spelling rules

In stressed syllables, the letters ai usually make the sound /eɪ/, as in (wait) /weɪt/. Before certain consonants, the letters ai make the short sound /ɛ/, as in (said) /sɛd/ or (air) /ɛər/. In unstressed syllables at the end of a word, this pair makes the weak sound /ə/, as in (captain) /kæp.tən/ and (curtain) /kɜːr.tən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not read each letter separately as two vowels. Glide smoothly through the main sound instead of stopping halfway. In unstressed endings, do not say the long sound /eɪ/. Keep the final vowel very weak and short.
articles.summary: This is the letter L319 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: oa
articles.body:
## Sounds of oa

The letters oa sound like /oʊ/. You hear this in the word (oak) /oʊk/, a large forest tree. This pair makes two different sounds in English words.

## Mouth movements

For the first sound, open your mouth slightly and push your lips forward into a circle. Then glide into a smaller circle. For the second sound, pull your tongue back, drop your jaw, and make an open round shape. Hold the vowel steady. Touch your throat to feel your voice buzz throughout both sounds.

## Spelling rules

In most words, these letters make the sound /oʊ/. You hear it inside (boat) /boʊt/ and (road) /roʊd/. When the letter r follows right after, they make the sound /ɔː/. You hear this pattern inside (roar) /rɔːr/ and (board) /bɔːrd/.

## Common mistakes

Do not freeze your mouth on one flat vowel for the main sound. Glide smoothly from an open vowel to a small circle. Before r, do not say two separate vowel sounds. Blend them into one long, open sound.
articles.summary: This is the letter L320 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: oo
articles.body:
## Sounds of double o

The letters oo are called the sound /ʊ/ or /uː/. Their main sound is the sound /uː/, heard in (moon) /muːn/, which means the bright round object in the night sky. These letters have four sounds in total.

## How to say double o

To make the first sound, push your lips tight into a small circle. Pull your tongue back and high. For the second sound, loosen your lips slightly. Keep your tongue high but relaxed. For the third sound, open your mouth halfway and relax your tongue. For the fourth sound, drop your jaw lower and round your lips. Feel your vocal cords buzz on your throat for all four sounds.

## Spelling of double o

The letters oo usually make the sound /uː/ before l, m or n, as in (cool) /kuːl/. They make the sound /ʊ/ mostly before k or d, as in (book) /bʊk/. In very few special words, they sound like /ʌ/, as in (blood) /blʌd/. Before r, they sound like /ɔː/, as in (door) /dɔː/.

## Common mistakes with double o

Do not make every word sound long. A short vowel needs loose lips and a relaxed tongue. Do not swap the vowel of foot with the long vowel of boot. Keep your lips soft and open your jaw a little wider.
articles.summary: This is the letter L321 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: ou
articles.body:
## The sound of ou

The letters ou usually sound like the sound /aʊ/. You hear this main sound in the word (out) /aʊt/, which means outside. This letter pair has four different sounds in English words. Most words use the first sound.

## How to say ou

To say the first sound, open your mouth wide. Then move your lips into a small round circle. For the second sound, push your lips far forward into a tight circle. For the third sound, keep your mouth slightly open and relaxed. For the fourth sound, make a very quick weak sound with relaxed lips. Touch your neck to feel your voice buzz.

## Spelling rules for ou

In most stressed syllables, ou makes the sound /aʊ/, as in (loud) /laʊd/. In borrowings and several common words, ou sounds like /uː/, as in (group) /ɡruːp/. Before consonants in some native words, ou makes the sound /ʌ/, that is a short stressed sound, as in (touch) /tʌtʃ/ or (cousin) /kʌz.ən/. In unstressed endings, ou sounds like the weak sound /ə/, that is a quick relaxed sound, as in (famous) /feɪ.məs/.

## Common mistakes with ou

Do not turn the main vowel sound into a single flat vowel. Start wide and glide smoothly to a round lip shape. Do not make the weak ending sound too strong. Keep that unstressed ending very short and quiet.
articles.summary: This is the letter L322 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: ow
articles.body:
## Sound of ow

The letters ow make two different sounds. Their main sound is the sound /aʊ/, as in the word (owl) /aʊl/. An owl is a night bird. Listen carefully to each word to learn which sound fits.

## How to say it

For the first sound, open your mouth wide. Then pull your tongue up and round your lips into a small circle. For the second sound, start with your mouth half open. Move your lips forward into a small circle as you finish. Put a hand on your throat to feel the strong vibration.

## Spelling rules

The letters ow most often make the sound /aʊ/ before consonants or at the end of words, as in (cow) /kaʊ/. They make the sound /oʊ/ as an alternative at the end of words, as in (snow) /snoʊ/. They also make the sound /oʊ/ before certain consonants, as in (bowl) /boʊl/.

## Common mistakes

Do not shorten the sounds into a single flat vowel. Always glide smoothly toward a small round lip shape. Do not mix up the two sounds in words with similar letters. Practice the change of lip shape slowly.
articles.summary: This is the letter L323 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: ie
articles.body:
## Sounds of ie

The letters ie are spoken as the sound /aɪ/ or the sound /iː/. Their main sound is the sound /aɪ/, heard in the word (pie) /paɪ/, meaning pie. These letters produce three different sounds in English words.

## How to say ie

For the first sound, open your mouth wide and glide your tongue upward. For the second sound, smile slightly, stretch your lips, and raise your tongue high. For the third sound, keep your mouth slightly open and relax your tongue. Put your hand on your throat to feel your voice buzz continuously for each vowel sound.

## Spelling of ie

At the end of short words, these letters make the sound /aɪ/, as in (tie) /taɪ/. Inside words, they usually make the long sound /iː/, as in (brief) /briːf/ or (chief) /tʃiːf/. In some words, they make the short relaxed sound /ɪ/, as in (sieve) /sɪv/.

## Comparing ie sounds

Learners often confuse the long vowel with the short vowel. Do not make the long sound /iː/ too short. Do not make the relaxed sound /ɪ/ too tense like the sound in see. Keep your tongue relaxed and lower for the short sound.
articles.summary: This is the letter L324 from the vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: au
articles.body:
## The letters au

The letters au sound like /ɔː/. You hear this main sound in (author) /ɔː.θər/, a person who writes books. Together, these two letters make three different sounds.

## Making the sounds

For the first sound, round your lips into an open circle. Pull your tongue back low, and let your voice hum. For the second sound, drop your jaw open wide without rounding your lips. For the third sound, keep your jaw open and round your lips just a little. Feel your throat vibrate with each vowel sound.

## Reading the letters

The letters au usually make the long sound /ɔː/ before consonants, as in (pause) /pɔːz/. In a few words from other languages, they sound like /ɑː/, as in (aunt) /ɑːnt/. They also make the short sound /ɒ/ in common words like (sausage) /sɒ.sɪdʒ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not pronounce both letters one after the other. Do not say the letters like two separate vowels. Always blend them into one steady sound. Keep your tongue steady until you finish speaking the vowel.
articles.summary: This is the letter L325.

articles.title: oi
articles.body:
## Sound of oi

The letters oi usually make the sound /ɔɪ/. You hear this in the word (oil) /ɔɪl/, which means oil. This spelling has two different sounds in English.

## How to say oi

To make the first sound, round your lips and open your mouth. Then glide your lips into a smile and raise your tongue. To make the second sound, round your lips tight, then open your mouth wide. Rest your hand on your throat to feel your voice buzz throughout both sounds.

## Spelling of oi

In most English words, these letters make the sound /ɔɪ/. You hear this sound in (coin) /kɔɪn/. In words borrowed from French, the letters make the sound /wɑː/. You hear this sound in the word (memoir) /mɛm.wɑː/.

## Common mistakes with oi

Do not split the sound into two separate vowels. Glide smoothly from the open shape to the smile. In borrowed words, do not say the usual vowel sound. Remember to shape your lips like a w at the start.
articles.summary: This is the letter L326.

articles.title: oy
articles.body:
## Sound of oy

The letters oy sound like /ɔɪ/. You hear this sound in the word (boy) /bɔɪ/, which means a young male person. These letters have only one sound in English.

## How to say oy

Start with your lips open and round. Your tongue sits low and pulled back. Then spread your lips wide into a smile. Your tongue glides up toward the front of your mouth. Keep your vocal cords vibrating all the time. Place two fingers on your throat to feel the steady buzz.

## Spelling of oy

The letters oy always make the sound /ɔɪ/. You find them at the end of words or before a vowel. A clear example is the word (toy) /tɔɪ/. They keep this exact pronunciation in every word.

## Comparing oy

Do not turn this into two separate sounds. Smooth the glide from open lips to a smile in one breath. Do not drop the final part, or it sounds like the vowel in law. Keep your voice smooth all the way through.
articles.summary: This is the letter L327.

articles.title: ar
articles.body:
## Sounds of ar

The letter group ar is spoken as the sound /ɑːr/. Its main sound is the sound /ɑː/, heard in (arm) /ɑːm/, which means arm. This letter group makes four different sounds in English words.

## How to say ar

Open your mouth wide and keep your tongue low and flat for the first sound. Drop your jaw fully, then pull your tongue tip slightly back for the second sound. Relax your mouth and tongue completely into the middle for the third sound. Round your lips firmly and pull your tongue back for the fourth sound. Feel your throat vibrate with your voice.

## Spelling rules for ar

In stressed syllables before a consonant, ar makes the sound /ɑː/, as in (car) /kɑː/. Before a vowel, ar makes the sound /ɑːr/, as in (starry) /stɑː.ri/, or in (far) /fɑːr/. In unstressed syllables, it makes the sound /ə/, as in (sugar) /ʃʊɡ.ə/, or in (dollar) /dɒl.ə/. After a w sound, it often makes the sound /ɔː/, as in (war) /wɔː/, or in (warm) /wɔːm/.

## Common mistakes with ar

Speakers often use the wrong vowel after a w sound. Do not say the open vowel of car in those words. Round your lips into the sound of talk instead. In unstressed syllables, do not give this group a full vowel. Keep it completely weak and relaxed.
articles.summary: This is the letter L328.

articles.title: er
articles.body:
## Sounds of er

The letters er make the sound /ɜːr/, as in the word (fern) /fɜːrn/. A fern is a green plant with feathery leaves. This letter combination makes two different sounds in English words.

## How to say er

For the first sound, keep your mouth slightly open. Pull your tongue back and curl the tip slightly up without touching anything. Make a long voice sound and feel your throat vibrate. For the second sound, relax your whole mouth completely. Make a very short, weak voice sound with your tongue resting in the middle.

## Spelling rules for er

In stressed syllables, the letters er sound like /ɜːr/, as in (term) /tɜːrm/. In unstressed syllables, usually at the end of a word, they sound like /ər/, as in (water) /wɔː.tər/ and (butter) /bʌ.tər/.

## Common mistakes

Do not roll your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Keep the tongue pulled back and still. In weak endings, do not make a strong vowel sound. Keep the ending very soft and quick.
articles.summary: This is the letter L329.

articles.title: ir
articles.body:
## Sound of ir

The letters ir make the main sound /ɜːr/, as in (bird) /bɜːrd/, which means bird. These letters have three sounds.

## How to say ir

For the first sound, keep your mouth half open, curl your tongue back slightly, and voice the sound. For the second sound, relax your tongue and lips completely, making a very short vowel. For the third sound, open wide, move to a smile, then curl your tongue back. Feel your vocal cords buzz in your throat for all three.

## Spelling of ir

In stressed syllables, ir makes the sound /ɜːr/, as in (shirt) /ʃɜːrt/. In unstressed syllables, ir makes the short sound /ər/, as in (elixir) /ɪ.lɪk.sər/. Before a silent e, ir makes the sound /aɪ.ər/, as in (fire) /faɪ.ər/ and (wire) /waɪ.ər/.

## Common mistakes

Do not roll your tongue when you say these sounds. Keep your tongue steady inside your mouth without tapping your teeth. Do not swap the long sound with a pure vowel like the sound in cat or pot. Always let the vowel blend smoothly into the r sound.
articles.summary: This is the letter L330.

articles.title: or
articles.body:
## The letters or

The letters or make the main sound /ɔːr/, as in (fork) /fɔːrk/. This word means a tool with points for eating food. These letters make three different sounds.

## Making the sounds

For the first sound, pull your tongue back and make your lips into an open circle. For the second sound, relax your tongue and lips completely in the middle of your mouth. For the third sound, hold your tongue flat and slightly curled while keeping your lips relaxed. Feel your voice box shake in your neck for all three sounds.

## Spelling patterns

In stressed parts of a word, these letters make the sound /ɔːr/, like in (corn) /kɔːrn/. In unstressed parts of a word, they make the weak sound /ər/, like in (doctor) /dɑːk.tər/. After the letter w, they make the sound /ɜːr/, like in (word) /wɜːrd/.

## Common mistakes

Do not drop the curling tongue motion at the end. In a word like (storm) /stɔːrm/, do not make your lips into a tight circle like in boot. Keep the mouth wider and let the air flow steadily.
articles.summary: This is the letter L331.

articles.title: ur
articles.body:
## Sounds of ur

The letters ur are called /ɜːr/. Their main sound is the sound /ɜːr/, as in (fur) /fɜːr/, which means fur. These letters have three sounds.

## How to say ur

For the first sound, keep your tongue relaxed in the middle of your mouth. Round your lips slightly and use your voice. For the second sound, make a very short, weak vowel. Relax your jaw, lips, and tongue completely. For the third sound, start with your tongue high, then pull it back and round your lips. Feel your vocal cords vibrate on your throat.

## Spelling rules for ur

In a stressed syllable before a consonant or at the end of a word, ur makes the sound /ɜːr/, as in (burn) /bɜːrn/. In an unstressed syllable, ur makes the weak sound /ər/, as in (sulphur) /sʌl.fər/. When silent final e follows, ur makes the sound /jʊər/, as in (cure) /kjʊər/.

## Common mistakes

Do not roll or tap your tongue against your teeth. Keep your tongue back in your mouth. Do not open your mouth too wide for the sound /ɜːr/. Keep your jaw steady and your lips slightly relaxed. In an unstressed syllable, do not put heavy stress on the vowel. Keep the sound short and very light.
articles.summary: This is the letter L332.

articles.title: bl
articles.body:
## Sound of bl

The letters bl sound as /bl/. Listen to this sound in (black) /blæk/, which means black. This letter pair makes only one sound combination in English.

## How to say bl

Close both lips firmly to stop the air. Release them gently while placing the tongue tip behind your upper front teeth. Let the air flow smoothly around the sides of your tongue. Turn on your voice for both parts. Feel your vocal cords vibrate in your throat.

## Spelling of bl

The letters bl always make the sound /bl/ at the beginning of a syllable. You hear this sound pattern in the word (blue) /blu/ and in (blind) /blaɪnd/.

## Common mistakes with bl

Do not insert a short vowel between the two letters. Move smoothly from your lips directly into the tongue position without a pause.
articles.summary: This is the letter L333 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: br
articles.body:
## The sound br

The letters br make the blended sound /br/. You hear this sound in the word (brown) /braʊn/, which means brown. These two letters always make this single combined sound.

## Mouth movements

Press your lips together to stop the air. Release them with your voice. At the same time, pull the tip of your tongue slightly back and curl it up. Touch a hand to your throat to feel the strong buzzing.

## Reading the letters

The letters br appear everywhere as the sound /br/. You see this sound at the start of the word (brick) /brɪk/.

## Common mistakes

Do not roll your tongue against your teeth. Keep your tongue tip back so the sound stays smooth. Do not add a vowel between the two letters.
articles.summary: This is the letter L334 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: cl
articles.body:
## Sound of cl

The consonant cluster cl makes the sound /kl/. Hear it in the word (clap) /klæp/, which means clap. This letter group makes one combined sound.

## Mouth movement

Press the back of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Release a burst of air without using your voice. Then quickly place the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth. Let voiced air flow around the sides of your tongue. Feel your vocal cords vibrate on that second step.

## Spelling rules

The spelling cl represents the sound /kl/ in all positions. You hear it at the start of words like (club) /klʌb/.

## Common mistakes

Do not insert a short vowel sound between the two consonants. Move your tongue smoothly from the back to the front without stopping.
articles.summary: This is the letter L335 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: cr
articles.body:
## Sound of cr

The letters cr make the sound /kr/. You hear this in the word (crab) /kræb/, which means crab. This letter pair makes only one sound.

## Mouth movements

Press the back of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Release a quick puff of air without using your voice. Then pull your tongue tip back slightly into your mouth, curling it up without touching the roof. Turn your voice on for the second part. Feel your throat vibrate on the second sound.

## Spelling rules

The letters cr appear at the start of words before a vowel. They make the sound /kr/ in (cross) /krɒs/.

## Common mistakes

Do not tap or roll your tongue against your teeth. Keep your tongue pulled back inside your mouth so it touches nothing. Do not add an extra vowel sound between the two consonants.
articles.summary: This is the letter L336 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: dr
articles.body:
## Sound of dr

The letters dr make the sound /dr/. You hear this sound in the word (drum) /drʌm/, which means drum. These two letters together have only one sound in English.

## Making the sound

Press the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth. Release the air while pulling your tongue back into your mouth. Slightly round your lips as you do this. Your vocal cords vibrate for the whole sound. Place a hand on your throat to feel the steady vibration.

## Spelling patterns

The letters dr always make the sound /dr/. You find this cluster at the beginning of words like (drop) /drɒp/ and (dress) /drɛs/.

## Common mistakes

Do not add a vowel between the two letters. Blend the two sounds smoothly together. Do not roll your tongue tip. Pull your tongue back without tapping the roof of your mouth.
articles.summary: This is the letter L337 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: fl
articles.body:
## The sound fl

The letters fl sound like /fl/. You hear this sound at the start of (flag) /flæɡ/, which means a piece of cloth with a pattern. This letter combination makes one sound blend.

## How to say fl

Touch your lower lip gently with your top front teeth. Blow air through the gap without using your voice. Then place the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth. Drop your tongue while turning on your voice. You can feel air on your hand first, then a vibration in your throat.

## Spelling rules

The letters fl appear in almost all positions. They always make the blended sound /fl/, as in the word (flat) /flæt/.

## Common mistakes

Do not insert an extra vowel sound between the two parts. Keep the flow smooth and quick. Do not stop the breath before moving your tongue. If you speak clearly, the transition feels natural.
articles.summary: This is the letter L338 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: gr
articles.body:
## The group gr

The letters gr make the sound /ɡr/. You hear this in the word (green) /ɡriːn/, which means green. This letter group makes only one sound.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Release the air with your voice. Then quickly pull your tongue back and curl the tip slightly backward without touching the roof. Keep your vocal cords vibrating throughout the whole sound. Place your hand on your throat to feel the steady vibration.

## Spelling rules

The letters gr always make the sound /ɡr/ when they appear together at the start or inside a word. You can hear this in the word (great) /ɡreɪt/. Another example is the word (grow) /ɡroʊ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not roll or tap your tongue against the front roof of your mouth. Never let the tongue tip touch the upper gum. Simply pull the tongue back and keep the sound smooth.
articles.summary: This is the letter L339 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: st
articles.body:
## The sound st

This letter group sounds like /st/. You hear it in the word (stop) /stɒp/, which means to cease moving. The group has two different sounds.

## How to say it

First, hiss air softly over your tongue tip near your upper teeth. Next, tap your tongue against the roof of your mouth. For the other sound, just hiss the air softly without tapping your tongue. Hold a hand to your throat to feel that your voice stays quiet.

## Spelling rules

Most of the time, this pair sounds like /st/. You hear this at the end of (fast) /fɑːst/. In some words before letters like l e, the second letter stays silent. Then the group sounds like /s/, as in (castle) /kɑː.səl/. It also sounds like /s/ before e n, as in (listen) /lɪs.ən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not add an extra puff of air after the second letter. Also, do not pronounce the second letter when it should be quiet. There is no other common pitfall.
articles.summary: This is the letter L340 from the alphabet vowel-consonant groups.

articles.title: What a Syllable Is
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, every beat of a word is a syllable. Each syllable has one vowel sound at its center. This vowel gives the syllable its loud voice. Listen to (mama) /ˈma.ma/, which means mother. You hear two beats. Each beat holds one vowel.

## How to say it
Open your mouth for each vowel. Do not rush through the vowel sound. In (mama) /ˈma.ma/, your voice stresses the first beat. Your pitch rises a little on that first beat. Then, your mouth makes the second beat softly. Keep both vowel sounds clear and steady.

## Reading rules
Count the vowel letters to find the syllables. One vowel sound makes one syllable. Look at (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water. It has two vowel sounds and two syllables. Consonants attach to the vowel. The vowel is always the main heart of each syllable.

## Common mistakes
Do not drop the vowel sound at the end of a word. Every syllable needs its vowel. Do not swallow vowels or blur them together. In (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house, say both beats fully. Give each syllable its own distinct, open sound.
articles.summary: Every syllable in Romanian builds around exactly one clear vowel sound.

articles.title: Open Syllables in Romanian
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the word (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house. Both parts end in a vowel. We call this an open syllable. The vowel sound does not stop quickly. You hold the sound pure and clear until the end. Listen to (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water. Each vowel rings out with full tone.

## How to say it
Open your mouth and let the sound flow freely. Do not block your breath with your tongue or lips. Keep your jaw relaxed and steady. Make the vowel firm and steady from start to finish. In (casă) /ˈka.sə/, stress the first part strongly. Keep your pitch steady while the final vowel fades softly.

## Reading rules
Divide a word between a vowel and the next consonant. When a single consonant sits between vowels, it starts the next part. Notice (masă) /ˈma.sə/, which means table. The first syllable ends with the vowel a. The second syllable ends with the vowel ă. Every open syllable ends directly on its vowel letter.

## Common mistakes
Do not cut the vowel short. Do not add an extra tiny sound at the end. A vowel in an open syllable must stay clean. Do not let your tongue glide like in the word 'go'. In (casă) /ˈka.sə/, keep each vowel pure. Give the final vowel its full time without dropping it.
articles.summary: Learn how to hold vowels clearly and cleanly at the end of open syllables in Romanian.

articles.title: Closed Syllables
articles.body:
## The sound
A closed syllable ends with a consonant sound. Listen to the word (pământ) /pəˈmɨnt/, which means earth. The last syllable ends with two consonants. Every ending consonant makes a crisp, clear sound. You must not swallow or drop the sound at the end.

## How to say it
Open your mouth for the vowel first. Then close your mouth firmly to finish the consonant. Listen to the word (om) /om/, which means man. Your lips touch completely for the final sound. Keep your breath steady until the syllable stops. Release the sound cleanly without adding an extra vowel.

## Reading rules
Look at the letters at the end of a syllable. When you see a consonant, read it with full energy. Listen to (lac) /lak/, which means lake. The letter sound does not fade away. In Romanian, you pronounce every written consonant firmly. Stress does not change this rule.

## Common mistakes
Do not swallow the final consonant. Do not soften it too much or let it disappear. Also, do not add an extra vowel at the end. Say (pământ) /pəˈmɨnt/ with a sharp final stop. Finish each sound cleanly before you move to the next word.
articles.summary: In Romanian closed syllables, pronounce the ending consonant clearly and do not drop it.

articles.title: Stress Is Free
articles.body:
## The sound
Stress gives extra power to one syllable.
That stressed beat sounds louder and longer.
In Romanian, stress can fall anywhere in a word.
Listen to (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water.
The stress is on the first part.
Now listen to (băiat) /bəˈjat/, meaning boy.
The stress moves to the end.

## How to say it
Push more air from your lungs on the strong syllable.
Open your mouth slightly wider on its vowel.
Make that vowel clearer and hold it a tiny bit longer.
Keep the unstressed syllables relaxed and softer.
Do not rush, and let the strong beat stand out naturally.

## Reading rules
Romanian writing usually does not show stress marks.
There is no fixed rule for which syllable gets the beat.
Because of this, stress can change the whole word.
Therefore, you must learn the stress for each new word you meet.
Always listen carefully to the speaker or dictionary audio.

## Common mistakes
Do not place stress on the same syllable in every word.
For example, do not always hit the first or last syllable.
Saying (băiat) /bəˈjat/ with stress at the beginning sounds wrong.
Check the stress when you learn a word.
Treat the stress as part of the spelling.
articles.summary: Romanian stress can land on any syllable, so you must learn the stress with every new word.

articles.title: Stress on the Last Syllable
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, many words carry the strong beat on the last syllable. You hear this beat clearly at the very end of the word. Listen to (ajuns) /aˈʒuns/, which means arrived. The final part sounds louder and stronger. This gives the language a steady rhythm.

## How to say it
Start the word with a relaxed mouth. Push more air from your lungs on the final syllable. Raise your voice pitch slightly on that last part. Make the last vowel longer and clearer. Listen to (copil) /koˈpil/, which means child.

## Reading rules
Many Romanian words end in a consonant. These words often place the stress on the last syllable. Words that describe past actions usually do this too. Look at the word (oraș) /oˈraʃ/, which means city. Notice how the stress falls right at the end.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress the first syllable of these words. If you stress the beginning, the word sounds strange. Keep the first vowels light and short. Save your energy for the end of the word. Keep your pitch steady until you reach the final sound.
articles.summary: Learn how and when to stress the final syllable of Romanian words clearly and correctly.

articles.title: Stress on the Second-Last Syllable
articles.body:
## The sound
Many Romanian words have a very regular beat. You often stress the second-last syllable. This beat sounds natural and rhythmic. Listen to the word (copilul) /koˈpi.lul/, which means the child. The middle beat is the loudest. Your voice rises slightly on that part.

## How to say it
Count the parts of the word from the end. Push more air from your lungs on the second-last part. Keep your mouth open longer on its vowel. Make that vowel louder and slightly higher in pitch. Say the last syllable softly and quickly. Let your voice relax at the very end.

## Reading rules
Two-syllable words often take stress on the first part. Listen to (masă) /ˈma.sə/, which means table. You also hear this pattern in (fată) /ˈfa.tə/, which means girl. When words grow longer with endings, the stress often stays on the second-last syllable. Look at word endings to find the rhythm easily.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress every syllable with equal power. That makes your speech sound flat and robotic. Also, do not always push stress onto the very last vowel. When you say (copilul) /koˈpi.lul/, do not stress the final part. Keep the last sound light and short.
articles.summary: Many Romanian words carry strong stress on the second-last syllable, which creates a clear and steady rhythm.

articles.title: Stress on the Third-Last Syllable
articles.body:
## The sound
You count syllables from the end of a word. In some words, you stress the third-last syllable. Listen to (muzică) /ˈmu.zi.kə/, which means music. Your voice climbs and sounds stronger on that part. The remaining syllables drop in power. This pattern gives long words a lively rhythm.

## How to say it
Open your mouth clearly on the stressed vowel. Push more air from your lungs. Make that syllable louder and slightly longer. Let your pitch rise a little bit. Then, relax your mouth for the final syllables. Do not stop the air between the parts. Keep the sound flowing smoothly to the very end.

## Reading rules
Look at long words with care. Many words place the stress near the end. Notice the word (fotografie) /fo.to.ɡraˈfi.e/, which means photograph. Here, the strong beat lands near the end. However, other words pull the beat back to the third-last syllable. Listen closely to each word to learn its beat.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress every syllable with equal force. Give only one syllable the main beat. Do not push the stress too far forward. In (fotografie) /fo.to.ɡraˈfi.e/, keep the force on the correct part. Do not drop the final vowels completely. Keep your tongue relaxed and speak without rushing.
articles.summary: Learn how to find and pronounce stress on the third-last syllable in Romanian words.

articles.title: Stress Is Not Written
articles.body:
## The sound
In every word, one syllable is stronger. You give it more power. You say it slightly louder and longer. Listen to (limbă) /ˈlim.bə/, which means language. The first part is strong. The voice falls on the second part. Stress gives the word its natural rhythm.

## How to say it
Open your mouth a little wider on the stressed syllable. Push more air from your lungs. Do not change the vowel sound. Keep every vowel clean and clear. For (copil) /koˈpil/, which means child, push air on the second syllable. Your tone rises slightly on the strong part, then drops softly.

## Reading rules
Standard letters never show where the stress goes. You cannot see a stress mark in normal texts. Because of this, you must listen carefully. You can also check a good dictionary. Dictionaries mark the strong vowel for you. Always learn a new word together with its sound.

## Common mistakes
Do not guess the stress pattern. Many learners stress the wrong syllable. If you say (limbă) /ˈlim.bə/ with stress at the end, it sounds wrong. Do not look for written accent marks on the page. Instead, rely on audio recordings. Train your ears to catch the beat every time.
articles.summary: Romanian letters do not mark stress, so you must use audio and dictionaries to find the strong syllable.

articles.title: Two Vowels in One Syllable
articles.body:
## The sound
Sometimes, two vowels meet in one beat.
They glide together smoothly.
You hear one quick sound instead of two separate beats.
Listen to the word (soare) /ˈso̯a.re/, which means sun.
The vowels blend into one voice push.
They stay close inside the same syllable.

## How to say it
Start with your lips rounded or tongue high.
Then, glide smoothly into the next open vowel.
Do not stop the air between them.
Keep the voice flowing in one breath.
Listen to (ploaie) /ˈplo̯a.je/, which means rain.
One vowel is strong and clear.
The other vowel is very quick and light.

## Reading rules
When you see two vowels together, look closely.
Often, they share one single syllable.
One vowel takes the main beat.
The other vowel acts like a fast slide.
In (iarnă) /ˈjar.nə/, the first sound glides into the next.
Read them as one smooth unit.
Never split them apart.

## Common mistakes
Do not separate the two vowels.
If you break them, you create an extra syllable.
That breaks the rhythm of the word.
Do not pause your voice in the middle.
Glide quickly from the first vowel to the second.
Keep your mouth moving in one continuous motion.
Let the sounds melt together easily.
articles.summary: Learn how two vowels glide together into one smooth syllable in Romanian words like ploaie.

articles.title: Hiatus Splits Vowels
articles.body:
## The sound
Sometimes two vowels stand right next to each other. You do not slide them into one sound. Instead, you say each vowel cleanly in its own beat. Listen to (România) /ro.mɨˈni.a/, which means Romania. The last two sounds do not melt together. You make two clear vocal beats at the end.

## How to say it
Open your mouth for the first vowel. Keep your voice strong and steady. Then, quickly move your lips and tongue to the second vowel. Do not drop your breath between them. Listen to (aer) /ˈa.er/, which means air. Your tone stays steady as your mouth changes shape for each sound.

## Reading rules
When two written vowels split into two syllables, pronounce both fully. One vowel usually takes more stress than the other. In (România) /ro.mɨˈni.a/, the voice rises slightly on the first vowel of the pair. The final vowel is softer. Give each letter its own time and clear shape.

## Common mistakes
Do not crush the two vowels into one quick glide. People often blend them like the sound in 'boy'. In Romanian, keep the vowels separate. Do not insert an extra puff of air between them either. Move smoothly from one vowel directly into the next without stopping your voice.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce neighbouring Romanian vowels as separate sounds in different syllables.

articles.title: Final -ă Stays Clear
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the letter ă at the end of a word. It sounds like the last sound in 'sofa'. You hear it clearly. It never disappears. Listen to the word (lampă) /ˈlam.pə/, which means lamp. The ending is soft, but you must say it completely.

## How to say it
Relax your mouth and keep your jaw slightly open. Keep your tongue flat in the middle of your mouth. Make a short, relaxed sound with your voice. Do not push your lips forward. Let the air flow out smoothly and gently.

## Reading rules
When you see the letter ă at the end, always pronounce it. Most words put the stress on the syllable before it. For example, listen to (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water. The first part is louder, but the last vowel is still clear and audible.

## Common mistakes
Do not swallow or drop the last sound. Some learners stop speaking too early and cut the word short. Never turn it into a sharp 'a' sound either. Keep it calm and distinct. Always finish the whole word with this gentle vowel.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the final vowel ă clearly without dropping it at the end of Romanian words.

articles.title: Stress Stays on the Root
articles.body:
## The sound
Stress means you say one part louder and longer. In many words, this strong part stays in the same place. Listen to (copil) /koˈpil/, which means child. Now listen to (copilul) /koˈpi.lul/, which means the child. The strong beat stays on the main part. The ending changes, but the beat does not move.

## How to say it
Open your mouth and push more air on the strong part. Say (copil) /koˈpil/ with more force on the second part. When you add an ending, keep that same force. Say (copilul) /koˈpi.lul/ smoothly. Do not push extra air onto the new ending. Keep your pitch steady on the added part.

## Reading rules
Look at the base of the word first. Find where the main stress lands. When you see a longer form of a noun, do not move the beat. Keep the stress right where it was before. The added letters at the end stay light and short. This rule helps you read new forms clearly.

## Common mistakes
Do not move the stress to the final letters. New learners often push hard on the new ending. If you say the ending too loud, listeners get confused. Always keep the main push on the root. Let the ending sound soft and quick. Relax your throat as you finish the word.
articles.summary: Learn why Romanian word stress stays on the root when a noun changes its form.

articles.title: Stress in Verb Endings
articles.body:
## The sound
Many Romanian action words put the stress at the very end. You hear the last beat ring out clearly. Listen to (vorbiți) /vorˈbit͡s/, which means you speak. The voice pushes hard on the final part. Hear it also in (citiți) /t͡ʃiˈtit͡s/, which means you read. The ending carries the loudest punch.

## How to say it
Start soft and save your energy for the end. Open your mouth wide for the final vowel sound. Give that final beat more time and volume. Make your pitch jump up slightly at the end. Do not rush past the word ending. Drop your energy only after you finish the word.

## Reading rules
Look closely at the word endings in written text. Endings often hold the main stress in these forms. When you see (mâncați) /mɨnˈkat͡s/, which means you eat, hit the end.
