The letters at the start stay short and light. Always direct your voice toward the final vowel. The strongest sound sits right there.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress the first syllable of the word. Many learners pull the stress forward by mistake. Never let the ending become quiet or weak. Keep the ending clear, loud, and proud. If you weaken the ending, people may misunderstand you. Always land firmly on that last beat.
articles.summary: Learn how to place the main stress on the final syllable of Romanian verb endings correctly.

articles.title: Feminine Adjectives and Stress Shift
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the masculine word (frumos) /fruˈmos/. It has two beats. The stress is at the end. Now listen to the feminine word (frumoasă) /fru.moˈa.sə/. The word grows longer. It gains an extra beat. The main stress shifts forward onto the new sound.

## How to say it
Start with the male form (frumos) /fruˈmos/. Your voice punches the last part: -mos. To say (frumoasă) /fru.moˈa.sə/, open your mouth wider in the middle. Slide from 'o' to 'a'. Put your loudest voice right on that vowel pair. End softly on the final sound.

## Reading rules
The letters o-a often make a sliding vowel sound. When you see the feminine ending, the beat changes. The letter ă sits at the end. It sounds like the first vowel in 'about'. Keep that last sound short and weak. Push the loudness onto the sliding vowels before it.

## Common mistakes
Do not keep the stress on the old masculine beat. If you say (frumoasă) /fru.moˈa.sə/ with old stress, people might not understand. Do not drop the final weak vowel. Give each beat its own time. Move your voice to the middle vowels and finish gently.
articles.summary: Learn how Romanian feminine adjectives add a syllable and move the stress to a new sound.

articles.title: Pronouncing the Endings -a and -ă
articles.body:
## The sound
Notice the last sound in (casă) /ˈka.sə/ and (casa) /ˈka.sa/.
The letter ă sounds relaxed and soft like the sound in 'comma'.
The letter a sounds bright, clear, and open like the sound in 'father'.
These two endings change the meaning completely.
One means a house, and the other means the house.

## How to say it
For ă, keep your mouth half open.
Relax your tongue in the middle of your mouth.
Make a short, quiet sound.
For a, open your mouth wide.
Drop your lower jaw.
Push your voice out clearly and cleanly.
Keep your lips relaxed for both sounds.

## Reading rules
Look closely at the little mark above the letter.
The letter ă with a bowl on top always makes a muffled sound.
The plain letter a always sounds clear and wide.
In (casa) /ˈka.sa/, the stress stays on the first part.
Do not move the stress to the end.

## Common mistakes
Do not pronounce the ending ă like an open a.
If you do, you say (casa) /ˈka.sa/ instead of (casă) /ˈka.sə/.
Also, do not stress the final vowel.
Keep the ending light and short.
Listen carefully to the difference and keep your jaw loose.
articles.summary: Learn the difference between the open sound in the ending -a and the relaxed sound in -ă.

articles.title: Unstressed Short Words
articles.body:
## The sound
Some short words do not have their own beat.
They sound light and weak.
Listen to (mă uit) /mə ˈu̯it/, which means I look.
The first tiny word has no loud beat.
It leans on the second word.
Together, they sound like one single word.
Your voice stays smooth without any stop between them.

## How to say it
Relax your mouth for the first word.
Keep your voice low and quiet.
Do not push air hard on it.
Then, glide quickly into the next word.
Make that second word louder and clearer.
In (mă uit) /mə ˈu̯it/, drop stress on the start.
Push energy only on the second part.
Your breath flows continuously across both words.

## Reading rules
You see two words in writing, but you read one sound unit.
Small helper words do not take the main stress.
They always bond with the action word that follows.
Another example is (te văd) /te ˈvəd/, which means I see you.
Read them together in one smooth breath.
Never pause between the two written words.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress the first word.
Do not say it with heavy force.
Never take a breath or stop between the words.
A break makes your speech sound stiff and choppy.
Do not pronounce the small word like an isolated unit.
Keep your mouth loose, and slide right into the next sound.
articles.summary: Short little words lose their stress and flow right into the next word.

articles.title: Stress in Long Words
articles.body:
## The sound
Long words can look scary. Many long words end with the ending -itate. Listen to (universitate) /u.ni.ver.siˈta.te/. Notice the loudest beat. The voice hits the syllable 'ta'. You hear this same beat in (calitate) /ka.liˈta.te/. The ending keeps the beat in the same spot.

## How to say it
Say the first parts of the word smoothly. Do not stop. Keep your voice steady. Then, make the syllable 'ta' stronger and higher. Drop your tone softly on the final syllable 'te'. Try it now with (activitate) /ak.ti.viˈta.te/. Your mouth stays relaxed until the strong syllable.

## Reading rules
When you read a word ending in -itate, look at the end. The strong beat always falls on the letter 'a' in that ending. It does not matter how long the word is. You always stress the syllable right before the last one.

## Common mistakes
Many people stress the start of a long word. Do not do that. Other people push the stress all the way to the very last letter. Remember (universitate) /u.ni.ver.siˈta.te/. The last sound is quiet. Always keep the strong beat on the syllable 'ta'.
articles.summary: Learn how to place the stress correctly on long Romanian words ending in -itate.

articles.title: Count Syllables and Mark Stress
articles.body:
## The sound
Words have rhythm. Each syllable is a beat. Listen to (dimineață) /di.mi.ˈɲa.tsə/, which means morning. It has four beats. One beat is louder and stronger than the others. We call this strong beat the stress.

## How to say it
Clap your hands for every beat in a word. Say (dimineață) /di.mi.ˈɲa.tsə/ slowly. Clap four times. Make the third beat louder and longer. Open your mouth wider on that beat. Let your voice jump higher there. The other beats stay soft and short.

## Reading rules
Look at (copil) /ko.ˈpil/, which means child. It has two beats. The stress lands on the second beat. Now look at (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water. The stress lands on the first beat. Romanian does not write stress marks on words. You must learn the rhythm of each word.

## Common mistakes
Do not make every beat equal. A flat rhythm sounds strange and robotic. Do not swallow the weak syllables. Say every beat clearly, even the soft ones. Always hit the stressed beat firmly. If you stress the wrong syllable, people might not understand you.
articles.summary: Learn to clap each Romanian syllable and emphasize the stressed beat for natural rhythm and clear pronunciation.

articles.title: Stress and Vowel Contrast
articles.body:
## The sound
Listen to the word endings carefully. A stressed ending sounds strong, clear, and long. An unstressed ending sounds light, quick, and soft. Listen to (vorbesc) /vorˈbesk/, which means I speak. The stress is on the last part. The vowel sounds clear. In (vorbește) /vorˈbeʃ.te/, meaning he speaks, the last vowel is soft and quick.

## How to say it
Open your mouth wider for a stressed ending. Push more air from your lungs. Make your voice higher and hold the vowel longer. For an unstressed ending, drop your jaw less. Use less air and keep your voice relaxed. Say (vorbesc) /vorˈbesk/. Hit the ending like the word 'desk'. Keep the sound punchy and bright.

## Reading rules
Romanian does not use written accent marks to show stress. You must learn which part gets the push. Verbs often put strong stress right on the final ending. Look at (vorbesc) /vorˈbesk/. The final letter e receives full power. Never hide or swallow a stressed ending vowel. Read it out loud with full energy.

## Common mistakes
Do not make every vowel equal in strength. Some learners say words flatly. In (vorbesc) /vorˈbesk/, do not stress the first part. Push only on the ending. Also, do not change stressed vowels into weak murmurs. Give the stressed vowel its pure sound. Keep unstressed endings softer, but keep stressed endings strong and crisp.
articles.summary: Learn how word stress changes vowel strength and quality at the ends of Romanian words.

articles.title: Practice: Stress in Pairs
articles.body:
## The sound
Every word has one strong beat. Your voice sounds louder and higher on this beat. Listen to (frumos) /fruˈmos/, which means beautiful. The beat lands on the end. When endings change, the strong beat often moves. You feel the rhythm jump to another part.

## How to say it
Open your mouth and push more air on the stressed part. Hold that vowel a little longer. Say word pairs together. Start with (cântă) /ˈkɨn.tə/. Hit the first part with extra force. Now say (cântăm) /kɨnˈtəm/. Push your voice forward and hit the new ending. Feel the beat jump.

## Reading rules
Written Romanian does not use stress marks. You cannot see the beat on paper. When a word adds an ending, the beat often moves. Read word pairs side by side. Train your ears to notice where the loud beat lands each time.

## Common mistakes
Do not keep the beat in the same spot. Some learners freeze the stress on the first syllable. This makes words sound flat or wrong. Do not make every syllable equally loud. Relax your mouth on the weak parts. Move the loud beat when the ending changes.
articles.summary: Practice moving the strong stress to the new ending when saying Romanian word pairs aloud.

articles.title: Soft C Before E and I
articles.body:
## The sound
The letter c makes a soft sound here.
It sounds like the first sound in 'church'.
Listen to the word (cer) /ˈtʃer/, which means sky.
You also hear it in (cine) /ˈtʃi.ne/, which means who.
The sound is crisp and clear.

## How to say it
Touch the roof of your mouth with your tongue tip.
Put it just behind your top front teeth.
Push air out and release your tongue quickly.
Do not use your vocal cords.
The air bursts through with a soft hiss.
Keep your lips slightly rounded as you speak.

## Reading rules
Look at the letter right after c.
Pronounce this soft sound whenever c comes before e or i.
Hear it at the start of (ce) /tʃe/, which means what.
This rule always works when you see ce or ci together.
Other letters after c make a hard sound instead.

## Common mistakes
Do not make a hard k sound before these vowels.
Do not say an s sound like in 'city'.
Start firmly with your tongue touching the roof of your mouth.
Keep the burst quick and neat.
Release the sound cleanly before you say the vowel.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the soft Romanian letter C before E and I like the sound in 'church'.

articles.title: Hard C Before A, O, U
articles.body:
## The sound
The letter c makes a crisp sound. It sounds like the 'k' in 'keep'. Listen to the word (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house. You hear a clear, hard sound at the start. Your breath stops completely for a moment. Then you release the air quickly.

## How to say it
Raise the back of your tongue. Press it firmly against the roof of your mouth. Do not use your voice yet. Build up air behind your tongue. Now, drop your tongue to let the air out. Listen to (copil) /koˈpil/, which means child. Keep the sound dry and short.

## Reading rules
Look at the letter right after c. Say this sound when c comes before a, o, or u. Hear it in (curat) /kuˈrat/, which means clean. The vowel changes, but the first sound stays firm. Do not change this sound before these three letters. It never softens here.

## Common mistakes
Do not add a heavy puff of air. Keep the release tight and neat. Also, do not make a 'ch' sound. That sound happens before other letters. Practice with (casă) /ˈka.sə/. Keep your tongue relaxed after the burst. Keep the sound clean and simple every time.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the Romanian hard c sound correctly before the vowels a, o, and u.

articles.title: Soft G Before E and I
articles.body:
## The sound
The Romanian letter g can make a soft sound.
It sounds like the first sound in 'jump'.
You hear it in the word (gene) /ˈdʒe.ne/, which means eyelashes.
You also hear it in (gem) /dʒem/, which means jam.
It is smooth, voiced, and energetic.

## How to say it
Touch the roof of your mouth with your tongue tip.
Stop the air for a tiny moment.
Then, release the air gently with friction.
Turn on your voice box to make it buzz.
Push your lips forward just a little bit.
Keep your tongue relaxed after the release.

## Reading rules
Look at the letter right after g.
The letter g makes this soft sound before e and i.
See it in (gene) /ˈdʒe.ne/.
The vowel follows right after without a pause.
Before other letters, g sounds hard like in 'go'.
Always check the next letter first.

## Common mistakes
Do not say a hard sound like in 'get'.
Before e and i, the sound must stay soft.
Do not add an extra sound between letters.
Keep the syllable tight and clean.
Do not whisper this sound.
Your vocal cords must buzz every time.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the soft Romanian letter g before e and i like the sound in 'jump'.

articles.title: Hard G Before A, O, U
articles.body:
## The sound
This sound is a hard consonant.
It sounds like the first sound in the word 'go'.
Your voice box vibrates when you make this sound.
Listen to the word (gară) /ˈɡa.rə/, which means station.
You also hear it in (gol) /ɡol/, which means empty.
The sound stays clean and steady.

## How to say it
Open your mouth slightly.
Lift the back of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth.
Stop the air at the back for a moment.
Then release the air quickly with your voice.
Do not add a puff of extra breath.
Listen to (gură) /ˈɡu.rə/, which means mouth.
Start the first syllable with firm energy.

## Reading rules
The letter g makes this hard sound before three vowels.
Look for the letters a, o, or u after g.
Whenever you see ga, go, or gu, pronounce a plain hard sound.
You read (gară) /ˈɡa.rə/ with this rule.
You also read (gol) /ɡol/ and (gură) /ˈɡu.rə/ with this same hard sound.

## Common mistakes
Do not make a soft sound like 'j'.
Never slide your tongue forward into a hiss.
Keep the back of your tongue pressed firmly before the release.
Also, do not blow out too much air.
Release the sound smoothly into the next vowel, like in (gară) /ˈɡa.rə/.
Keep your vocal cords vibrating from the start.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the hard Romanian g sound before the vowels a, o, and u.

articles.title: The Letters Ghe and Ghi
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, the letter group *gh* makes a hard sound.
It sounds like the 'g' in 'go' or 'get'.
You hear it in (ghem) /ɡem/, which means ball of yarn.
You also hear it in (ghici) /ˈɡi.tʃi/, which means to guess.
The sound is always firm and voiced.

## How to say it
Open your mouth a little bit.
Press the back of your tongue against the roof of your mouth.
Build up air behind your tongue.
Release the air quickly and vibrate your vocal cords.
Do not blow extra breath through your mouth.
Keep the sound short, crisp, and clean.

## Reading rules
The letter *h* is silent here.
It only protects the hard sound before *e* and *i*.
Write *ghe* to get a hard sound before *e*.
Write *ghi* to get a hard sound before *i*.
Listen to (ghid) /ɡid/, which means guide.
Without *h*, the letter *g* sounds soft.

## Common mistakes
Do not pronounce the letter *h*.
The *h* has no sound of its own here.
Do not say a soft sound like 'j' in 'jam'.
Always keep the sound hard like 'gift'.
Practice with the word (ghici) /ˈɡi.tʃi/.
Keep your tongue firm at the back for every word.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the hard Romanian consonant sound written with ghe and ghi before vowels.

articles.title: Pronouncing Romanian Che and Chi
articles.body:
## The sound
The letters c and h work as a team. Together, they make one clean, crisp sound. You hear this sound in the word (chiar) /kjar/, which means really. It sounds like the first sound in 'keep'. The sound is sharp and light. It never sounds like 'church'.

## How to say it
Lift the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Press it flat and firm. Stop the air for a brief moment. Then, release the air quickly with a sharp puff. Keep your voice quiet and do not buzz your throat. Smile slightly to help your tongue find the right place.

## Reading rules
Look for the letter h right after the letter c. You only see this sound before the vowels e or i. Listen to the word (chem) /kem/, which means I call. Now listen to (chip) /kip/, which means face. The letter h stays silent. It only tells you to keep the c sound crisp and hard.

## Common mistakes
Do not make a rough sound in your throat. Do not make the sound from 'chat'. Many learners try to pronounce the letter h by itself. Never blow air for the letter h here. Treat the two letters as one single sound. Keep the sound forward in your mouth at all times.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the letters che and chi in Romanian as a crisp, single sound.

articles.title: The Sounds Ș and Ț
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the letters ș and ț.
They have a small comma below.
The letter ș sounds like 'sh' in 'shoe'.
Hear it in (școală) /ʃkoˈa.lə/, which means school.
The letter ț sounds like 'ts' in 'cats'.
Hear it in (țară) /ˈt͡sa.rə/, which means country.

## How to say it
Push your lips forward for ș.
Blow air softly over your tongue.
For ț, touch the roof of your mouth with your tongue tip.
Stop the air for a moment.
Then quickly release it with a sharp hiss.
Keep your voice quiet and smooth for both sounds.

## Reading rules
These two letters never change their sound.
You see ș, you always say 'sh'.
You see ț, you always say 'ts'.
Vowels after them do not alter their sound.
Even at the end of a word, keep the sound clear.
Do not confuse them with plain s or t.

## Common mistakes
Do not pronounce ș like a simple s.
Do not pronounce ț like a simple t.
Both letters need their full hiss.
Notice the little comma under the letter.
Without the comma, the letter makes a different sound.
Pay close attention to these marks when you read.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the Romanian letters ș and ț clearly and correctly every time.

articles.title: Plural t becomes ț
articles.body:
## The sound
The letter ț makes a sharp sound.
It sounds like the end of 'cats'.
When one thing becomes many, the sound changes.
A single brother is (frate) /ˈfra.te/.
Two or more are (frați) /frat͡sʲ/.
The flat t sound turns into a sharp ț sound.

## How to say it
Place the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth.
Build up air pressure.
Then, quickly release the air through a narrow gap.
Make a quick 'ts' sound.
Do not use your voice box for this sound.
Keep the air stream short and crisp.
Push your lips slightly forward as you speak.

## Reading rules
Look at the letter ț with a small comma below it.
In many plurals, the last t changes into ț before the final letter i.
Listen to the word (băieți) /bəˈjet͡sʲ/, which means boys.
The final letter i is very soft and short.
You barely hear it after the ț sound.

## Common mistakes
Do not say a regular t in these plurals.
Saying (frați) /frat͡sʲ/ with a plain t sounds wrong.
Also, do not make a long vowel at the end.
Keep the final sound quick and sharp.
Do not separate the t and s into two steps.
Blend them into one single quick burst of air.
articles.summary: When many Romanian words become plural, the consonant t shifts to the sharp ț sound.

articles.title: How T Becomes Ț in Plurals
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the word for boy, (băiat) /bəˈjat/.
When you make it plural, it becomes (băieți) /bəˈjet͡sʲ/.
The regular "t" sound changes into a "ts" sound.
It sounds like the end of the word 'cats'.
The sound is sharp, crisp, and short.
Your voice does not buzz.

## How to say it
Put the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth.
Build up a small puff of air.
Release the air quickly through a narrow gap.
You hear a quick hiss, like 'ts'.
At the end of (băieți) /bəˈjet͡sʲ/, do not make a full vowel.
Just soften the sound with your tongue.

## Reading rules
In writing, the letter changes from "t" to "ț".
The letter "ț" has a small mark underneath.
This letter always makes the "ts" sound.
Plural words often add a final "i".
When "t" meets this plural ending, it becomes "ț".
You hear this clearly in (băieți) /bəˈjet͡sʲ/.

## Common mistakes
Do not keep the hard "t" sound in the plural.
Never say the ending like 'tea'.
The final letter "i" is almost silent here.
Do not pronounce a long vowel at the end.
Keep the "ts" sound light and short.
Listen carefully to the ending of (băieți) /bəˈjet͡sʲ/.
articles.summary: Learn how the sound T changes into a TS sound in Romanian plural words.

articles.title: Plural C Becomes CI
articles.body:
## The sound
In one tree, (copac) /koˈpak/, the word ends with a 'k' sound.
In many trees, (copaci) /ko.paˈt͡ʃʲ/, the sound changes.
The letter 'c' now sounds like 'ch' in 'chin'.
The ending is very short and soft.
You release a tiny puff of air.

## How to say it
Put your tongue tip behind your upper teeth.
Press your tongue against the roof of your mouth.
Stop the air for a brief moment.
Then push the air out gently.
Keep your voice box quiet.
Do not add a full vowel at the end.

## Reading rules
Look at the word (copac) /koˈpak/.
It ends with the letter 'c'.
To make it plural, you add an 'i'.
The letters 'ci' make the 'ch' sound.
Do not make a long vowel sound here.
The stress stays on the syllable /pa/.

## Common mistakes
Many learners keep the hard 'k' sound.
Do not say 'k' when you see 'ci'.
Another mistake is adding a loud vowel sound.
The final sound is not 'chee'.
It is just a short, whispered 'ch' sound.
Drop your voice smoothly at the end.
articles.summary: When many Romanian words become plural, the final k sound turns into a soft ch sound.

articles.title: Vowel Change O to OA
articles.body:
## The sound
Listen to (floare) /ˈflo̯a.re/, which means flower.
Notice the two letters run together.
You hear a glide from an o-sound into an a-sound.
In the plural (flori) /ˈflorʲ/, this glide turns back to a simple sound.
The sound shifts when the word ending changes.

## How to say it
Start with your lips rounded for a quick 'o'.
Open your jaw quickly into a clear 'ah' sound.
Do not make two separate beats.
Keep the stress on the open vowel.
Your voice glides smoothly in one single pulse.
Practice with the word (floare) /ˈflo̯a.re/.

## Reading rules
When you see the letters o and a together, read one sound.
Many singular words use this sound before an open ending.
Look at (floare) /ˈflo̯a.re/ again.
When the plural ending arrives, the sound often shortens to a simple o.
Look at the plural form (flori) /ˈflorʲ/.
The letters show you the exact change.

## Common mistakes
Do not split the sound into two syllables.
Do not say 'o-ah' slowly.
Blend the two vowels into one quick glide.
Also, remember to change the sound back in plural forms.
Do not say the glide in (flori) /ˈflorʲ/.
Keep the plural vowel short and round.
articles.summary: Learn how the Romanian vowel o changes to oa in singular and plural words.

articles.title: The Letters Î and Â
articles.body:
## The sound
Two letters in Romanian make the very same vowel sound. These letters are î and â. You hear this sound in the word (români) /roˈmɨnʲ/, which means Romanians. It is a deep, central sound. Your voice stays steady and clear when you speak it.

## How to say it
Start to make the sound in the word 'see'. Now, pull your tongue back into the middle of your mouth. Keep your lips flat and relaxed. Do not round your lips. Push air through your throat with a steady voice. The sound comes from deep inside.

## Reading rules
Both letters make the exact same sound. You usually write â inside words, as in (români) /roˈmɨnʲ/. You write î at the start of words, as in (în) /ɨn/. You also see î inside words when a root word starts with it. The pronunciation never changes.

## Common mistakes
Do not round your lips when you say this sound. Rounded lips make a different vowel entirely. Also, do not pronounce the two letters differently. They sound identical. Practice with the word (români) /roˈmɨnʲ/ until your tongue feels natural. Keep your jaw relaxed every time.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the Romanian letters î and â with correct mouth shape and simple spelling rules.

articles.title: Pronouncing the Letter H
articles.body:
## The sound
The letter h makes an open breath sound.
It sounds like the h in 'hat' or 'hotel'.
Listen to the word (hotel) /hoˈtel/, which means hotel.
You also hear it in (hartă) /ˈhar.tə/, which means map.
The sound is always clear and light.
Air flows freely through your throat.

## How to say it
Open your mouth slightly.
Keep your tongue relaxed and low.
Do not touch your teeth or palate.
Breathe out gently from your throat.
Do not use your vocal cords.
You only make the sound with passing air.
Practice saying (hotel) /hoˈtel/ smoothly.
Push the breath out right before the vowel.

## Reading rules
You always pronounce this letter in Romanian.
It is never silent.
You see it at the start of words like (hotel) /hoˈtel/.
You also see it in words like (haină) /ˈhaj.nə/, which means coat.
Say it every time you see it written.
Make the breath sound before you say the next vowel.

## Common mistakes
Do not drop this sound.
Never leave the letter h silent like in 'hour'.
If you say (hotel) /hoˈtel/ without the h, people notice.
Also, do not scrape your throat too hard.
Keep the air soft and smooth.
Just exhale quietly and move directly into the vowel.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the letter h in Romanian as a clear, audible breath sound in words like hotel.

articles.title: Pronouncing X Between Vowels
articles.body:
## The sound
The Romanian letter x often sounds like two blended consonants. Between two vowels, it makes a buzzing sound. It sounds like the letters 'g' and 'z' joined together. Listen to the word (examen) /e.ˈɡza.men/, which means exam. You hear this soft, vibrating sound right in the middle.

## How to say it
Start with the back of your tongue touching your soft palate. Release a quick 'g' sound with your vocal cords buzzing. Then, move the tip of your tongue near your front teeth. Push air out smoothly to make a 'z' sound. Keep your voice box vibrating for the whole sound.

## Reading rules
Look at the letters around the letter x. When x sits between two vowels, say it as a buzzing sound. Listen to (exact) /eɡˈzakt/, which means exact. Also, listen to (exemplu) /eɡˈzem.plu/, which means example. In both words, vowels surround the letter x. Your voice stays on through both letters.

## Common mistakes
Do not whisper the sound like 'k' and 's'. Many learners turn off their voice too early. If you make a hiss, your voice box stops. Touch your throat while you speak. You should feel a strong vibration when you say (examen) /e.ˈɡza.men/.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the Romanian letter x as a voiced gz sound between two vowels.

articles.title: Letter S Before E and I
articles.body:
## The sound
The letter s makes a clear hissing sound.
It sounds like the first sound in 'sun'.
It never changes when other letters follow it.
Listen to (seară) /ˈse̯a.rə/, which means evening.
Hear the clear s sound at the start.
Now listen to (sete) /ˈse.te/, which means thirst.

## How to say it
Bring your teeth close together.
Keep your tongue behind your front teeth.
Do not let your tongue touch your teeth.
Blow air smoothly through the narrow gap.
Do not vibrate your vocal cords.
The sound is crisp, dry, and sharp.
Practice with the word (sigur) /ˈsi.ɡur/, which means sure.

## Reading rules
In some languages, s changes before certain vowels.
In Romanian, the letter s never changes its sound.
Before e, it stays a plain s.
Before i, it also stays a plain s.
You always read (seară) /ˈse̯a.rə/ with a crisp s sound.
Keep the sound the same everywhere.

## Common mistakes
Many learners change s into an sh sound before e or i.
Others turn it into a buzzing z sound.
Do not buzz your voice.
Do not round your lips.
Keep your lips relaxed and flat.
Always make a pure hissing sound, as in (sete) /ˈse.te/.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the letter s always keeps its plain hissing sound before the vowels e and i.

articles.title: Voiceless Consonants at Word Ends
articles.body:
## The sound
Some consonants make your throat vibrate.
Other consonants are quiet and airy.
At the end of a word, buzzing consonants lose their buzz.
They become quiet sounds.
Listen to (pod) /pot/, which means bridge.
The word ends with a letter for 'd'.
Yet you hear a clear 't' sound at the end.

## How to say it
Put your fingers gently on your throat.
Say a long 'z' sound.
You feel a vibration.
Now whisper an 's' sound.
The vibration stops completely.
When you say (brad) /brat/, meaning fir tree, stop the vibration at the end.
Press your tongue behind your teeth.
Release a quick puff of air with no voice.

## Reading rules
Look at the last letter of a word.
A written 'd' sounds like 't'.
A written 'b' sounds like 'p'.
A written 'g' sounds like 'k'.
For example, read (bob) /bop/, which means grain.
You see a final 'b'.
However, your lips pop with a dry 'p' sound.

## Common mistakes
Do not keep your vocal cords buzzing until the silence.
Many learners push voice into the final sound.
This can make words sound heavy and unnatural.
Keep the ending light and short.
Do not add an extra vowel sound after the last consonant.
Just cut off the voice and let air finish the word.
articles.summary: A voiced consonant at the end of a word turns into a voiceless consonant in Romanian pronunciation.

articles.title: Pronouncing Ce in Romanian Questions
articles.body:
## The sound
The question word (ce) /tʃe/ means what. It starts with a sound like 'ch' in 'check'. The vowel is like the 'e' in 'bed'. Together, you say /tʃe/. Listen to the phrase (ce faci) /tʃe ˈfatʃʲ/, which means what are you doing. The sound is crisp and quick.

## How to say it
Touch your tongue behind your top front teeth. Release the air quickly to make the first sound. Then, open your mouth a little for the vowel. Keep your lips relaxed and flat. Do not push your lips forward. Keep the vowel very short. Let your voice rise slightly to show a question.

## Reading rules
The letters c and e always make this sound together. When you see them at the start of a sentence, say /tʃe/. In questions, this word never takes heavy stress. Instead, the stress jumps forward to the next word. Look at (ce faci) /tʃe ˈfatʃʲ/. Here, your voice stresses (faci) /ˈfatʃʲ/.

## Common mistakes
Do not say a hard sound like 'k'. Do not pronounce it like 's' either. Another mistake is making the vowel too long. Some people say 'chay', like in 'say'. Never add that gliding sound at the end. Keep it short, flat, and light. Move your voice quickly to the next word.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the short Romanian question word ce clearly and naturally when you ask questions.

articles.title: Soft and Hard Sound Pairs
articles.body:
## The sound
Some letters change their voice in pairs. One sound is hard and deep. The other sound is soft and sharp. Listen to the hard start of (gară) /ˈɡa.rə/, station. Now hear the soft start of (ger) /ˈd͡ʒer/, frost. You train your ear to hear this shift.

## How to say it
Say the words out loud. For hard sounds, push air from the back of your throat. For soft sounds, lift your tongue toward your roof. Keep your jaw relaxed. Switch between the two sounds in a smooth rhythm. Feel the tongue move forward and back.

## Reading rules
Look closely at the vowel right after the letter. Letters like a, o, and u keep the sound hard. Letters like e and i make the sound soft. Read the pair slowly. Check the vowel first, then shape your mouth before you speak.

## Common mistakes
Do not rush through the words. Many learners make both sounds the same. That can change the meaning of your word. Also, do not add extra breath at the end. Keep every sound short and clean. Listen carefully as you switch from hard to soft.
articles.summary: Read word pairs aloud to hear and feel the difference between soft and hard Romanian sounds.

articles.title: Hyphenation: Split Words Between Syllables
articles.body:
## The sound
Words break naturally into small beats called syllables.
Listen to the beats in (ajutor) /a.ʒuˈtor/, which means help.
Each beat carries a vowel sound.
Your voice stays smooth across every beat.
The rhythm guides your breath.
You hear three clear beats in this word.

## How to say it
Open your mouth slightly for the first beat.
Push air forward gently for the second beat.
Stress the last beat firmly with a higher pitch.
Do not stop your breath between beats.
Let each sound flow into the next smoothly.
Say (ajutor) /a.ʒuˈtor/ as one flowing melody.

## Reading rules
Sometimes a line ends in the middle of a word.
You place a hyphen between two complete syllables.
Never break a single syllable apart.
For example, you write (ajutor) /a.ʒuˈtor/ across lines as a-ju-tor.
Another example is (carte) /ˈkar.te/, which splits as car-te.
A vowel always remains in each part.

## Common mistakes
Do not cut inside a single syllable.
Never leave a single consonant alone at the line edge.
Do not pause unnaturally when you read a broken word aloud.
Keep the rhythm steady and natural.
Read the whole word without a gap.
Treat it just like any regular word.
articles.summary: When you break a Romanian word across lines, always split it cleanly between syllables.

articles.title: Dividing Single Consonants in Romanian
articles.body:
## The Basic Rule
Romanian syllables follow clear and simple patterns. When one consonant sits between two vowels, it always joins the second vowel. This means the first syllable ends with an open vowel sound. Linguists call this an open syllable. The rule works everywhere in Romanian, whether at the start, middle, or end of words. Learning this rule helps you read new words smoothly. It also makes your rhythm sound natural.

## Mouth and Voice Flow
Keep your voice flowing smoothly between the sounds. Do not stop your airflow at the end of the first vowel. Let the vowel ring clearly before your mouth prepares the consonant. For example, your lips should close for the consonant only when starting the next beat. The vocal stress usually falls on the first part of common words. Say the stressed syllable with a slightly higher pitch, then drop your voice gently on the second beat.

## The Word Ma-mă
A classic example of this pattern is the word **ma-mă** /ˈma.mə/, which means mother. The letter **m** sits between the vowels **a** and **ă**. Following our rule, that middle consonant belongs entirely to the second syllable. You say **ma**, then you say **mă**. Stress the first syllable firmly. Your mouth opens wide for the first vowel, then your lips tap together to start the second syllable cleanly.

## Mistakes to Avoid
English speakers often pull the middle consonant backward into the first syllable. They might try to say *mam-uh*. That changes the natural rhythm of Romanian. Avoid closing your lips too early while saying the first vowel. Keep the first vowel open and pure. Give the consonant completely to the second syllable, and keep the final vowel short and relaxed.
articles.summary: When a single consonant stands between two vowels, it always moves to the second syllable.

articles.title: Short forms: n-a
articles.body:
## The sound
Two small words often melt together in fast speech. You drop a vowel sound. The word (nu) /nu/ joins the word (a) /a/. They become one quick sound. Listen to (n-a venit) /na veˈnit/, which means he did not come. The two words fuse cleanly into one.

## How to say it
Touch the roof of your mouth with your tongue tip for the first sound. Drop your jaw quickly into an open central vowel. Do not pause between the two parts. Speak it like the start of the English word 'nap'. Keep your voice flowing smoothly into the next word.

## Reading rules
You write this short form with a hyphen. The dash shows that a letter is gone. When you see this dash, do not stop your voice. Read both parts together as a single syllable. The stress usually moves forward onto the action word that follows it.

## Common mistakes
Many learners pause at the hyphen. Do not stop your breath there. Another mistake is saying the full sound (nu) /nu/ by accident. Always blend the letters into one quick breath. Keep the sound light and move quickly to the main word.
articles.summary: Learn how the words nu and a merge into the short form n-a in Romanian speech.

articles.title: Short Forms: Saying n-am
articles.body:
## The sound
People often speak fast.
Two words join together into one quick beat.
You take (nu) /nu/, which means not.
You add (am) /am/, which means I have.
They join together into (n-am timp) /nam tʲimp/.
This phrase means I do not have time.
The vowel sound drops completely.

## How to say it
Start with your lips open.
Press the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth.
Make a humming sound through your nose.
Drop your tongue at once and open your mouth wide.
Finish with closed lips.
Say (n-am timp) /nam tʲimp/ without any break.
Keep the flow smooth.

## Reading rules
Look at the spelling.
A hyphen joins the first letter to the next word.
The hyphen shows that a vowel is gone.
Do not pause at the hyphen.
Read the parts together.
Say (n-am timp) /nam tʲimp/ with steady speed.
Your voice stays smooth and moves forward quickly.

## Common mistakes
Do not stop in the middle.
Some learners pause where they see the hyphen.
Do not make two separate beats.
Never insert a tiny break between the sounds.
Keep your voice rolling across the words.
Treat the first part like the English word 'numb', but open your mouth wider.
articles.summary: Learn how Romanian shortens nu am to n-am in fast speech and how to pronounce it smoothly.

articles.title: Pronouncing the Clitic Mi-e
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, two short words often melt together. The unit (mi-e) /mje/ sounds like one fast beat. You hear an m sound, then a quick glide, and an open vowel. Listen to (mi-e frig) /mje frig/, which means I am cold.

## How to say it
Start with your lips closed for the first sound. Open your mouth quickly into the glide. Do not pause between the letters. Push your voice out in one single breath. Your tone stays smooth and fast. Say the whole unit quickly before you add (frig) /frig/.

## Reading rules
The hyphen shows that two words join together. You see two words, but you read one syllable. The first vowel becomes a quick glide like the 'y' in 'yes'. The second vowel takes the main energy. Whenever you read (mi-e) /mje/, never separate the parts.

## Common mistakes
Do not make two separate beats. Never say two slow vowels with a pause. A small break between the letters sounds unnatural. Another mistake is dropping the first vowel completely. Keep both sounds alive in your mouth. Squeeze them together into one quick burst of air.
articles.summary: Learn how two words join into one quick sound when you pronounce mi-e in Romanian.

articles.title: Pronouncing the Combined Word ți-e
articles.body:
## The sound
The mark between the letters joins two parts into one sound.
You say them together in one breath.
Listen to (ți-e foame) /tsje ˈfo.ame/, which means you are hungry.
The first sound starts sharp and flows directly into the vowel.
Your voice does not pause between them.

## How to say it
Put the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth.
Release air quickly with a sharp sound, like 'ts' in 'cats'.
Glide right into a quick 'y' sound and finish on 'e'.
Keep your jaw relaxed and your lips slightly open.
Say the whole cluster smoothly without any break.

## Reading rules
The hyphen shows that two words merge into one syllable.
Here, the pronoun (ți) /tsi/ connects directly to the verb (e) /e/.
The vowel in the first part weakens to a quick glide.
The stress moves forward to the next main word.
Read the written hyphen as a bridge, not a stop.

## Common mistakes
Do not say the two parts as two separate words.
Never stop your breath at the hyphen.
Also, do not drop the sharp start of the sound.
Keep the tongue close to the teeth.
Blend the sounds quickly, so the rhythm stays smooth and natural.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the combined form ți-e smoothly as a single quick syllable in Romanian.

articles.title: Pronouncing the Romanian Clitic i-a
articles.body:
## The sound
The letters (i-a) /ja/ sound like one quick syllable.
You hear a glide like the 'y' sound in 'yes'.
Then you hear an open 'ah' sound immediately.
In (i-a spus) /ja spus/, these two words link smoothly together.
The voice flows across them without any break.

## How to say it
Start with your tongue high and near the front.
Move smoothly down and open your mouth wide.
Do not stop the air between the sounds.
Keep the stress on the next word in (i-a spus) /ja spus/.
Say (i-a) /ja/ quickly, quietly, and with very light breath.

## Reading rules
You see a hyphen between the letters.
The hyphen shows that two small words become one sound unit.
The first letter is a helper word.
The second letter is also a helper word.
Together, read (i-a) /ja/ as one syllable.
Always link them into the main action word that follows.

## Common mistakes
Do not say two separate vowel sounds.
Do not pause at the hyphen.
Never stress (i-a) /ja/.
The louder beat belongs to the main word, as in (i-a spus) /ja spus/.
Keep your voice flowing forward smoothly into the full phrase.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the linked Romanian words i-a smoothly as one syllable without pausing at the hyphen.

articles.title: Saying Ce-ai as One Sound
articles.body:
## The sound
In fast speech, two words can join together. You hear one single syllable. The words (ce) /tʃe/ and (ai) /aj/ blend into (ce-ai) /ˈtʃaj/. It sounds like the start of 'chair' joined with 'eye'. The voice glides smoothly across the sounds. You do not stop between them.

## How to say it
Start with your tongue behind your top front teeth. Release the air quickly to make the first sound. Then, open your mouth wide. Quickly glide your tongue up and forward. Keep your voice strong and steady on the main vowel sound. Say the whole unit in one smooth breath.

## Reading rules
Look for a hyphen between the two parts. The written mark shows that two words become one sound. When you see (ce-ai) /ˈtʃaj/, read it without any break. The hyphen tells you to drop the first vowel sound. You blend the remaining consonant directly into the next word.

## Common mistakes
Do not pause between the two parts. Some people try to say each part slowly. That creates two separate beats and breaks the rhythm. Do not add an extra sound in the middle. Glide smoothly from start to finish. Keep the pitch natural and relaxed.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the blended Romanian phrase ce-ai smoothly as a single unit in natural speech.

articles.title: Pronouncing Nu-l in Romanian
articles.body:
## The sound
Two words join together into one quick beat. Listen to the phrase (nu-l văd) /nul vəd/. It means I do not see him. The middle vowel drops away completely. You say one smooth part instead of two. The voice glides through without any pause.

## How to say it
Start with rounded lips for (nu) /nu/. Then, quickly tap your tongue behind your front teeth. Do not make a new vowel sound. Keep your voice going strong. Say it in one quick breath. It rhymes closely with 'pool'.

## Reading rules
You see a hyphen between the two written parts. The full form begins with (îl) /ɨl/. The hyphen shows that the vowel drops. You read the two parts as one unit. Put your stress on the next main word.

## Common mistakes
Do not say two separate words here. People often stop their voice at the hyphen. Never take a breath between the letters. Also, do not add an extra vowel between them. Keep the sound short, tight, and connected. Move smoothly into the next word.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce nu-l smoothly as one connected sound in everyday Romanian speech.

articles.title: Pronouncing Dintr-o
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the hyphen in (dintr-o) /ˈdin.tro/.
The two parts fuse into one smooth unit.
You hear the consonant and the vowel flow together.
Listen to (dintr-o dată) /ˈdin.tro ˈda.tə/, which means suddenly.
The ending sound links without any gap.

## How to say it
Start by making the clean sound (dintr-o) /ˈdin.tro/.
Touch your tongue behind your upper teeth for the front sound.
Tap your tongue quickly for the rolling sound.
Round your lips right away for the final round vowel.
Keep the voice steady.
Do not add a pause between the letters.

## Reading rules
The hyphen shows a link between two words.
It drops the old vowel and pulls the next sound in.
Say the group as two clean beats.
Stress the first beat firmly.
Then, slide smoothly into (dată) /ˈda.tə/.
Read the whole phrase (dintr-o dată) /ˈdin.tro ˈda.tə/ with a single breath.

## Common mistakes
Do not stop at the hyphen.
Never insert a tiny pause between the consonant and the vowel.
Do not say two separate words.
Also, keep the stress on the first syllable of (dintr-o) /ˈdin.tro/.
Do not push the stress onto the last vowel.
Keep your rhythm quick, natural, and connected.
articles.summary: Learn how to connect the consonant and vowel smoothly in dintr-o without pausing at the hyphen.

articles.title: Saying într-o in Romanian
articles.body:
## The sound
Look at the phrase (într-o zi) /ɨn.tru ˈzi/, which means one day.
The word (într-o) /ɨn.tro/ has a small hyphen.
In fast speech, the last letter sounds very weak and light.
It shifts toward a quick sound like 'to'.
Both words flow together as one unit.

## How to say it
Start with your tongue in the center of your mouth.
Make the first sound firmly.
Then, relax your lips quickly for the ending sound.
Do not pause before the next word.
Put the main stress on the following word, like (zi) /zi/.
Your voice rises and hits the target word with energy.

## Reading rules
The hyphen shows two words written together.
It tells you not to stop your breath.
You see the letter 'o', but you speak it softly.
It connects smoothly to whatever word comes next.
You read the phrase as a single wave of sound.
The beat falls only on the second word.

## Common mistakes
Do not say two separate words with a stop.
Do not stress the letter 'o'.
If you say a loud 'o', it sounds heavy and robotic.
Keep the vowel brief and light.
Slide directly into the next sound without breaking the air.
Let your voice push forward to the end.
articles.summary: Learn how to say într-o smoothly by weakening the final vowel and connecting it to the next word.

articles.title: Pronouncing Mulțumesc in Spoken Romanian
articles.body:
## The sound
The standard word is (mulțumesc) /mult͡suˈmesk/. It means thank you. In everyday speech, people often shorten this word. You may hear the casual form (mulțam) /mulˈt͡sam/. Fast speech softens the sounds. The strong beat stays on the final syllable in both words.

## How to say it
Start with your lips relaxed. Touch your tongue to your upper teeth for the first sound. Then make a crisp sound like 'ts'. Push the stress to the end of the word. When you speak fast, do not stop between sounds. Keep the flow smooth and quick. Let your voice drop slightly at the end.

## Reading rules
The letters spell out every part of (mulțumesc) /mult͡suˈmesk/. The letter with a comma below makes a sharp 'ts' sound. The final group of consonants stays crisp in slow speech. In rapid conversation, speakers drop the middle sounds slightly. You can choose the full form or the short form (mulțam) /mulˈt͡sam/.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress the first syllable. Putting the beat too early sounds unnatural. Do not pause before the final consonants. Connect all vowels smoothly without adding extra breath. Also, do not force every single sound in casual talk. Relax your tongue so the word sounds natural and friendly.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the Romanian word for thank you and recognize its common shortened spoken forms.

articles.title: Saying Bună Dimineața Smoothly
articles.body:
## The sound
You say this greeting as one smooth phrase.
Listen to (bună dimineața) /ˈbu.nə di.mi.ˈɲa.tsa/, which means good morning.
Do not pause between the words.
Your voice flows from start to end without a break.
The strongest push of air lands on the final part of the phrase.

## How to say it
Start with relaxed lips and tongue.
Say (bună) /ˈbu.nə/ quickly and keep moving forward.
Do not stop your breath between the parts.
Slide your voice directly into the next word.
Push your breath harder on the very end.
Let your tone stay bright and welcoming.
Keep the whole phrase connected as one piece.

## Reading rules
Two written words often join into one spoken rhythm.
You see two words in print.
However, you say them like a single long unit.
The main stress always moves to the end of the greeting.
Give less weight to the first word.
Say the ending with more energy and clear voice.

## Common mistakes
Do not make a pause in the middle.
People often stop between the two words.
This break makes your speech sound robotic.
Do not stress the first word too much.
Keep the air moving until the last syllable.
Finish the greeting with a gentle, rising tone.
Practice saying the whole phrase in one breath.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the morning greeting as one continuous phrase with stress at the end.

articles.title: Fast Invitations with Hai and Să
articles.body:
## The sound
Listen to (hai) /haj/ and (să) /sə/.
Together with an action, they form an invitation.
Listen to (hai, să mergem) /haj sə ˈmer.dʒem/, meaning come on, let's go.
The first two words sound light.
The main beat lands on the end.

## How to say it
Keep your jaw relaxed for the start.
Glide quickly through (hai) /haj/.
Make (să) /sə/ very brief with a relaxed tongue.
Do not pause between these words.
Push your voice forward to the verb.
The tone stays quick and friendly.

## Reading rules
The letters in (hai) /haj/ sound like 'eye'.
The letter ă in (să) /sə/ sounds like 'a' in 'about'.
In print, you often see a comma after (hai) /haj/.
In speech, you do not stop at this comma.
Read the phrase as one smooth line.

## Common mistakes
Many learners stress every single word equally.
Do not make (hai) /haj/ loud or long.
Do not drag out (să) /sə/.
If you pause after each word, you sound stiff.
Keep the start soft and fast.
articles.summary: Keep the starting words short and light when you make a fast invitation in Romanian.

articles.title: Speech Rhythm: Unstressed Words
articles.body:
## The sound
Listen to short words like (în) /ɨn/ or (la) /la/.
These tiny words sound very light.
Your voice does not punch them.
Instead, you save your breath for the next word.
Together, they sound like one single word.
One part stays quiet, and the other part rings out loud.

## How to say it
Keep your voice soft on the first word.
Do not stop your airflow between the words.
Say (în casă) /ɨn ˈka.sə/, which means at home.
Glide right from the first sound into the second sound.
Your mouth stays relaxed at first.
Then, you push more air on the main syllable.

## Reading rules
When you read short words, keep moving forward.
Do not pause after words like (la) /la/.
Read them as a quiet step before the main beat.
In the phrase (în casă) /ɨn ˈka.sə/, stress only the first part of the last word.
The rhythm stays smooth and natural.

## Common mistakes
Do not hit every word with equal force.
If you say (în) /ɨn/ too loudly, the rhythm breaks.
Do not pause between the small word and the main word.
Keep the breath flowing without any stop.
Connect them like syllables inside one single word.
articles.summary: Short words carry very little stress and link smoothly to the stronger word that follows them.

articles.title: Stress in Mă Duc
articles.body:
## The sound
Listen to the phrase (mă duc) /mə duk/, which means I am going. You say two little words together. The first word is weak and quick. The second word is strong and clear. Together, they sound like one single word. Your voice pushes on the second part.

## How to say it
Start with the small word (mă) /mə/. Relax your mouth and keep your voice light. Make the sound very short. Now move quickly to the word (duc) /duk/. Round your lips for this part. Put all your energy here. Raise your pitch slightly on this final beat.

## Reading rules
When you see (mă duc) /mə duk/, do not stop between words. Read them as one smooth rhythm unit. The letter ă is a soft, resting sound. It never takes the stress in this phrase. The main beat always lands on the letter u.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress both words equally. If you emphasize the first word, you break the flow. Do not pause between the two parts. Do not make the first sound too loud or long. Keep the first beat weak and jump straight to the strong finish.
articles.summary: Learn how to connect the weak word mă and the strong word duc smoothly as one spoken unit.

articles.title: Pronouncing Nu Mai Quickly
articles.body:
## The sound
Listen to the phrase (nu mai) /nu maj/, which means no more. The word (nu) /nu/ means not. The word (mai) /maj/ means more. Together, they sound like one unit. You hear strong stress on (nu) /nu/. The following sound is weak and fast.

## How to say it
Start with your lips rounded for (nu) /nu/. Say it with a clear, steady voice. Next, move quickly to (mai) /maj/. Open your mouth for 'ah' and glide to 'ee'. Do not push extra air out. Keep the pitch high on (nu) /nu/ and drop it fast on (mai) /maj/.

## Reading rules
You see two words in writing: (nu mai) /nu maj/. In speech, you connect them without a pause. Treat them like one word with two parts. Put your main focus on (nu) /nu/. Glide through (mai) /maj/ very quickly. The two words always flow together like a single breath.

## Common mistakes
Do not pause between the two words. Some people give equal force to each part. That makes speech sound stiff and unnatural. Do not stress (mai) /maj/. If you make it strong, it sounds heavy. Say (nu) /nu/ clearly and let (mai) /maj/ follow weakly. Keep the pace brisk and natural.
articles.summary: Learn how to say (nu mai) /nu maj/ smoothly with weak stress on the second word.

articles.title: Fast Phrases and Weak Forms
articles.body:
## The sound
People speak fast in daily life. Small words lose their full strength. They join bigger words to make one smooth flow. Listen to (n-am timp) /nam tʲimp/, which means I do not have time. The little negative word links right to the verb. The weak word has no heavy stress.

## How to say it
Relax your mouth and jaw. Do not pause between the small words. Say (n-am timp) /nam tʲimp/ in a single breath. Place the main beat on the last word. Keep your tongue light on the first sound. Let the sounds flow together like one long word.

## Reading rules
A hyphen often shows a weak form in writing. The hyphen drops a vowel and joins two words. Look at the phrase (n-am timp) /nam tʲimp/. Here, (nu) /nu/ loses a vowel and joins (am) /am/. Read hyphenated pairs without stopping. Treat them as a single spoken unit.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress every single word equally. Do not stop at the hyphen. Some learners say each piece slowly and separate the sounds. This sounds stiff and robotic. Keep the first part soft and fast. Push the main energy toward the end of the phrase.
articles.summary: Learn how to link words smoothly and pronounce weak forms naturally at normal speaking speed.

articles.title: Falling Tone in Statements
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, a statement finishes on a low musical note. Your voice stays level during the sentence. Then, your voice slides down on the last word. Listen to (sunt) /ˈsunt/ (român) /roˈmɨn/, which means I am Romanian. The pitch drops clearly on the last beat.

## How to say it
Start speaking at a relaxed, medium pitch. Keep your tone steady on the first words. Find the last stressed syllable in the sentence. Let your voice fall gently to a low pitch. Relax your throat and chest as you finish. Say (român) /roˈmɨn/ with a falling slide.

## Reading rules
Look at the punctuation mark at the end. A period shows a complete idea and a falling tone. You drop your voice on statements. You also drop your voice when answering with (da) /ˈda/, which means yes. Only rise if you see a question mark. Otherwise, always glide down at the end.

## Common mistakes
Do not raise your voice at the end. A rising pitch makes a statement sound like a question. Do not drop your pitch too early either. Keep the pitch flat until the final stressed part. Finish firmly so the listener knows you are done.
articles.summary: Your voice drops at the end of a regular Romanian statement to show you finished speaking.

articles.title: Rising Tone in Yes-No Questions
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, you change your pitch to ask a simple question.
A yes-no question does not change word order.
Instead, your voice rises at the end.
Listen to (Ești român?) /ˈeʃtʲ roˈmɨn/, which means Are you Romanian?
The tone climbs smoothly on the final syllable.

## How to say it
Start speaking at your normal pitch.
Keep your pitch flat through the first words.
When you reach the last syllable, push your voice upward.
Make your tone climb higher like a musical note.
Open your throat and let the final sound ring clearly.
Do not drop your voice at the end.

## Reading rules
Look for a question mark at the end of the sentence.
Romanian questions often have the same word order as statements.
For example, (vine) /ˈvi.ne/ means he comes.
To ask a question, raise your pitch at the end.
The question mark signals that your voice must climb.

## Common mistakes
Many learners drop their pitch at the end of every sentence.
If your voice falls, the question sounds like a plain statement.
Do not rise too early in the sentence either.
Keep your voice level until the end.
Only lift your pitch on the final stressed part.
articles.summary: Learn how to raise your voice pitch at the end of Romanian yes-no questions to sound natural and clear.

articles.title: Falling Tone in Wh-Questions
articles.body:
## The sound
In Romanian, some questions start with a question word.
Listen to (unde) /ˈun.de/, which means where.
Your pitch starts high on the question word.
Then, your voice slides down until the sentence ends.
The pitch falls, just like in a simple statement.
It does not rise at the finish.

## How to say it
Start with extra energy on the first word.
Say the question word clearly.
Keep your lips relaxed as you speak.
Now practice the sentence (Unde locuiești?) /ˈun.de lo.kuˈi.eʃtʲ/, which means where do you live.
Stress the first word strongly.
Let your pitch drop gently on the last syllables.
Finish on a low, quiet note.

## Reading rules
Look at the start of the sentence.
Notice words like (ce) /tʃe/, which means what.
When a question begins with such a word, prepare to fall.
You see a question mark at the end.
Even with that mark, do not raise your tone.
Always let your voice step down at the end.

## Common mistakes
Many learners raise their voice at the end of every question.
Do not do that here.
A rising tone sounds like you expect a yes or no answer.
It makes your speech sound unsure or unfinished.
Keep the end low.
Drop your voice firmly when you reach the final syllable.
articles.summary: Your voice drops at the end of a Romanian question that begins with a question word.

articles.title: Exclamation Intonation
articles.body:
## The sound
An exclamation shows strong feeling. Your voice does not stay flat. Instead, your pitch jumps high on the most important word. Then, your voice falls quickly at the end. Listen to (Ce frumos!) /tʃe fruˈmos/, which means how beautiful. The music of the sentence feels lively and bright.

## How to say it
Start at a normal speaking pitch. When you reach the main word, push your voice upward. Make that stressed vowel higher and louder. Right after this peak, drop your pitch down fast. Try it with (Bravo!) /ˈbra.vo/, which means well done. Release plenty of breath on the peak.

## Reading rules
Look for an exclamation mark at the end of the sentence. Find the word that carries the biggest emotion. Raise your voice on the stressed syllable of that word. In (Ajutor!) /a.ʒuˈtor/, the voice climbs high on the last part. Then, let your voice drop immediately before you stop.

## Common mistakes
Do not keep your voice flat. A flat tone sounds bored or robotic. Do not rise at the very end like a question. The rise happens in the middle on the key word. After the rise, always let the tone fall down. Keep the drop clear and smooth.
articles.summary: Learn how to use rising and falling pitch to express strong feelings in Romanian exclamations.

articles.title: Saying Commands with Falling Tone
articles.body:
## The sound
A command tells someone to act right now. Your voice starts high and drops fast. The melody does not go up at the end. It falls down hard. Listen to (Vino aici!) /ˈvi.no aˈitʃʲ/, which means come here. The pitch drops sharply on the last part.

## How to say it
Push air quickly from your chest. Start the command with strong energy. Make the first stressed part loud and clear. Then, drop your pitch right away. Do not drag the sounds out. Listen to (Taci!) /tatʃʲ/, which means be quiet. Cut the final sound short and firm.

## Reading rules
Look for an exclamation mark at the end. This mark shows high energy and a direct order. Read the whole phrase in one breath. Never pause in the middle. Keep the rhythm quick and decisive. Your tone must fall all the way down.

## Common mistakes
Many people raise their voice at the end. That makes a command sound like a question. Do not let your pitch rise. Another mistake is speaking too slowly. Do not stretch the ending. Keep the final sound short, flat, and low. A command must sound crisp and firm.
articles.summary: Learn how to speak Romanian commands with a crisp rhythm and a sharp falling tone.

articles.title: Lists and Commas
articles.body:
## The sound
When you list items, your pitch changes. Each item before the end has a short rising tone. This rise shows that more items are coming. The very last item has a falling tone. This fall tells your listener that the list is finished.

## How to say it
Start with an even rhythm. Raise your pitch slightly on each item before a pause. This small rise links the words together. On the final item, drop your voice down. Listen to (Am pâine, lapte și ouă) /am ˈpɨ.i.ne ˈlap.te ʃi ˈo.u̯ə/. Your voice rises twice and drops once.

## Reading rules
Commas in a list tell you where to pause briefly. When you see a comma, make your voice go up slightly. The linking word introduces the last item. Do not raise your pitch on that final word. Instead, let your voice fall with the period.

## Common mistakes
Do not make your tone flat across the whole list. A flat tone sounds unnatural and boring. Also, avoid rising on the final item. A rising end turns your statement into a question. Drop your voice firmly at the end.
articles.summary: Your voice rises slightly on each listed item and drops on the final item.

articles.title: Dashes in Dialogue
articles.body:
## The sound
A dash does not make a sound by itself. Instead, it shows that a person starts talking. You pause briefly before you speak. Your voice often rises or sounds lively when speech begins. Listen to (Bună) /bu.ˈnə/, which means hi. The dash before it signals fresh, spoken words.

## How to say it
Stop for a tiny moment at the dash. Take a breath and lift your pitch slightly. Speak the first word with fresh energy. In (Bună) /bu.ˈnə/, keep your voice warm and clear. Your tone should sound friendly and natural. Then continue smoothly with the rest of the sentence.

## Reading rules
Look at the start of a written line. A long dash marks direct speech in text. You do not see quotation marks here. When someone answers, a new line starts with another dash. For example, an answer can be (Da) /da/, which means yes.

## Common mistakes
Do not look for quotation marks around spoken turns. Dashes replace them at the start of lines. Do not read without a tiny pause at the dash. A short break helps the listener hear the shift. A short reply like (Nu) /nu/, which means no, needs this clear start.
articles.summary: Learn how dashes mark spoken dialogue in Romanian text and how to pause when reading them aloud.

articles.title: Romanian Quotation Marks
articles.body:
## The sound
Quotation marks show someone is speaking. They do not make a sound by themselves. Instead, they guide your tone. Your voice pauses slightly before quoted speech. Then your pitch changes to show spoken words. Listen to the greeting „(bună) /bu.ˈnə/!”. Your voice sounds bright and friendly here.

## How to say it
Pause briefly when you see the opening quote. Drop your voice slightly before the quote starts. Raise your pitch inside the quote to sound lively. For „(da) /da/”, push clear air through your open mouth. Stress the quoted word clearly. Lower your pitch again after the closing quote.

## Reading rules
Look closely at the marks on the page. The opening quote sits low on the baseline. It looks like two tiny commas. The closing quote sits high at the top. It looks like two raised apostrophes. Read „(pa) /pa/” with quotes around it to show a clear goodbye.

## Common mistakes
Do not place the opening quote up high. It always sits down at the bottom line. Do not read quoted words in a flat voice. A flat tone sounds like a robotic list. Give the quoted word real life with your pitch. Pause at the marks to let the listener breathe.
articles.summary: Learn how Romanian quotation marks sit on the line and how to change your voice when reading them.

articles.title: Oare in Questions
articles.body:
## The sound
You use (oare) /ˈo.a.re/ when you wonder about something. It turns a statement into a question of doubt. Listen to (Oare vine?) /ˈo.a.re ˈvi.ne/, which means "I wonder if he is coming?". Your pitch goes up at the start. It stays high until the end.

## How to say it
Round your lips for the first sound in (oare) /ˈo.a.re/. Open your mouth wide for the next sound. Put the stress on the first syllable. Your voice rises on (oare) /ˈo.a.re/. Keep your tone rising gently to the end of the sentence. Do not let your pitch drop.

## Reading rules
Look for (oare) /ˈo.a.re/ at the beginning of a question. The letters "o" and "a" make two distinct vowel sounds. Say them smoothly together without a break. When you see this word, prepare for a rising question tune. It shows that the speaker is not sure.

## Common mistakes
Do not drop your pitch at the end of the question. A falling tone makes the sentence sound like a flat statement. Keep the melody rising to show true doubt. Also, do not blend the vowels into one flat sound. Pronounce both vowels clearly in (oare) /ˈo.a.re/.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce the word oare in Romanian questions of doubt using a rising tone.

articles.title: Ellipsis and Pauses in Romanian
articles.body:
## The sound
Three dots mark a pause in Romanian speech.
Your voice slows down before the silence.
The pitch stays level or floats downward gently.
Your speech sounds unfinished on purpose.
You hesitate, think, or show doubt.
Listen to (Ei... nu știu) /ej nu ʃtʲiu/, which means well, I do not know.

## How to say it
Keep your lips and tongue relaxed.
Do not drop your pitch suddenly.
Hold the vowel slightly longer before you stop speaking.
Leave your mouth slightly open during the pause.
Let your breath trail away softly into silence.
Then start the next part with fresh air and a calm tone.

## Reading rules
Look for three dots in a row in written text.
This mark tells you to stop making sound for a moment.
The mark acts like a long comma.
Your voice does not finish like a period.
Instead, your tone hangs in the air while you wait.

## Common mistakes
Do not rush past the three dots.
People often skip the pause and say every word together.
Do not drop your pitch hard like the end of a sentence.
A sudden drop sounds final and certain.
Keep your voice level so the listener waits for your next word.
articles.summary: Learn how to pause and trail your voice when you see three dots in Romanian.

articles.title: Pausing for Dashes and Parentheses
articles.body:
## The sound
Dashes show an extra thought inside a sentence.
Your voice changes around them.
You make a very short pause before the dashes.
You make another short pause after them.
Inside the dashes, your voice pitch drops a little bit.
It sounds like a quiet side note.

## How to say it
Start the first part of your sentence normally.
Stop your breath for a quick split second.
Lower your pitch slightly for the words between the dashes.
Speak those words a little bit faster.
Pause again for a brief moment.
Then, raise your pitch back to normal and finish.

## Reading rules
Look for long dashes or brackets in text.
They set words apart from the main sentence.
Say (Vine — spune el — mâine) /ˈvi.ne spuˈne el ˈmɨ.i.ne/, which means he is coming tomorrow.
You pause briefly before and after the middle part.
Never link those words directly to the rest.

## Common mistakes
Do not rush through the dashes without stopping.
If you skip the pauses, the sentence sounds confusing.
Also, do not raise your pitch inside the dashes.
A higher pitch makes the phrase sound like a question.
Keep your pauses short and your voice tone low.
articles.summary: Pause briefly before and after dashes, and drop your voice pitch slightly for the words inside.

articles.title: Rhythm of Stressed Syllables
articles.body:
## The sound
Romanian rhythm relies on strong beats. Stressed syllables sound clear and loud. Unstressed syllables pass by quickly. Listen to (mulțumesc) /mul.t͡suˈmesk/ (mult) /mult/, which means thank you very much. The beat falls firmly on the loud parts. The weak parts move fast and light.

## How to say it
Push more air from your lungs on stressed beats. Open your mouth wider on those parts. Say the unstressed parts with less breath. Do not stop between beats. Let your voice bounce smoothly from beat to beat. Keep your pitch natural and lively.

## Reading rules
Every word has one main beat. Find the stressed vowel first. Give that vowel extra time and strength. Read the word (bine) /ˈbi.ne/, which means well. The first part is long and strong. The second part is short and quiet. Move through the quiet vowels quickly.

## Common mistakes
Do not give every part equal weight. Speech is not flat like a ticking clock. If you make every vowel loud, you sound stiff. Do not drop unstressed vowels completely either. Keep them short, but do not swallow them. Balance strong beats with light, quick sounds.
articles.summary: Learn how stressed syllables create Romanian rhythm while unstressed syllables stay quick and light.

articles.title: Conditional Sentences with a Pause
articles.body:
## The sound

This melody connects two parts of a conditional sentence.
Your voice changes direction at the pause.
In the first part, your tone climbs slightly at the end.
In the second part, your tone drops to finish the thought.
Listen to (dacă) /ˈda.kə/ (vrei) /vrej/, (vino) /ˈvi.no/.

## How to say it

Start with relaxed lips and tongue.
Say the first clause and lift your pitch near the comma.
Hold the last syllable a bit longer before you pause.
Do not close your throat during the tiny rest.
Then, speak the second clause.
Let your pitch fall steadily until your voice rests quietly at the end.

## Reading rules

A comma in writing usually marks this change in pitch.
Sentences that begin with condition words like (dacă) /ˈda.kə/ use this pattern.
The comma tells you to pause and raise your musical pitch slightly.
After the comma, read the conclusion with falling pitch.
A period at the end marks your lowest pitch.

## Common mistakes

Do not drop your voice before the comma.
A falling pitch makes the sentence sound finished too early.
Do not raise your voice at the final period either.
A rising end sounds like a question.
Keep the rise small in the first part and fall clearly at the very end.
articles.summary: Raise your pitch before the pause in a conditional sentence, then let it fall steadily to the end.

articles.title: Emphasis by Word Order
articles.body:
## The sound
You can change word order to show what is important.
The most important word moves to the front.
This first word sounds louder and clearer than the rest.
Your pitch rises slightly on this first word.
Then, your voice drops and stays lower for the words that follow.

## How to say it
Push more air from your lungs on the first word.
Speak this word with a stronger voice.
Listen to (Eu sunt) /ˈe.u sunt/, which means it is me.
Your tone rises on the first vowel sound.
Then, your voice falls on the second word.
Drop your lower jaw gently and finish softly.

## Reading rules
Look at the start of the Romanian sentence.
The most important information usually comes first.
When you read, place the main stress right at the beginning.
In (Eu sunt) /ˈe.u sunt/, stress the first word heavily.
The second word stays quiet.
Word order shows the listener where your focus is.

## Common mistakes
Do not stress every word with equal force.
If you stress both words, you lose the clear emphasis.
Do not raise your pitch at the end like a question.
Keep the second word soft and low.
Also, do not rush the opening word.
Give that first word enough breath and time.
articles.summary: Learn how putting the most important Romanian word first gives it the strongest stress and tone.

articles.title: Polite requests with vă rog
articles.body:
## The sound
You use (vă rog) /və ˈroɡ/ to say please.
This phrase sounds soft and gentle.
Your voice does not jump up at the end.
Instead, the pitch falls slightly on the last part.
Keep your voice warm and friendly.
A gentle fall sounds very polite in Romanian.

## How to say it
Start quietly with the short word (vă) /və/.
Relax your mouth and make a quick sound like 'a' in 'sofa'.
Then say (rog) /roɡ/ with more weight.
Round your lips for the middle vowel.
Let your pitch drop gently on this second word.
Smile softly to keep the tone kind.

## Reading rules
The letter ă in (vă) /və/ is a relaxed sound.
Never say it as a hard vowel.
In (rog) /roɡ/, the letter o sounds like 'or' without the r.
The letter g at the end is hard, like in 'go'.
Put the main stress on the second word.

## Common mistakes
Do not raise your pitch like a question.
A rising tone can sound surprised or rude.
Do not push the air out too hard.
If you speak too loudly, you lose the gentle feeling.
Keep (vă rog) /və ˈroɡ/ soft, smooth, and low at the end.
articles.summary: Learn how to say the polite Romanian phrase for please with a soft, falling tone.

articles.title: Asking for Agreement with Nu
articles.body:
## The sound
You use (nu) /nu/ at the end of a phrase to ask for agreement.
Your voice rises quickly at the very end.
Listen to the phrase (Vii, nu?) /ˈvi.i nu/, which means you are coming.
The musical pitch jumps up high on this last word.
It asks the listener to agree with you.

## How to say it
First, say your statement with a level or falling pitch.
Pause for a tiny moment before the end.
Touch your tongue behind your top teeth for the first sound.
Then round your lips tightly for the vowel.
Push your pitch upward like a step on stairs.

## Reading rules
You always see a comma before the word (nu) /nu/.
A question mark stands right after it.
The comma tells you to pause briefly.
The question mark signals your voice to rise.
Whenever you spot this ending, lift your tone high.

## Common mistakes
Do not let your pitch fall at the end.
A falling pitch makes it sound like a negative statement.
Do not rush through without a tiny pause.
Make sure your lips stay rounded for the vowel.
Keep the vowel clear as your voice climbs upward.
articles.summary: Learn how to ask for agreement by adding the rising word nu at the end of a sentence.

articles.title: Short Romanian Calls and Tone
articles.body:
## The sound
You use short calls to get attention or show surprise. Listen to (hei) /hej/, which means hey. Listen to (ei) /ej/, which means well. These words are quick. They have a lively musical rise or fall. Your voice carries emotion in these little sounds.

## How to say it
Open your mouth for the first vowel sound. Move your tongue quickly up for the glide. For (hei) /hej/, push air out gently for the first sound. Keep the vowel clean. Raise your pitch at the end to call a friend. Drop your pitch to show doubt.

## Reading rules
The letter h sounds like the start of 'hat'. The letters e and i join together in one quick pulse. You see this in (hei) /hej/ and (ei) /ej/. Do not split the letters into two beats. The tone changes with the punctuation mark after them.

## Common mistakes
Do not say two separate syllables. Do not stretch the vowel too long. Speak with energy, not a flat voice. In (hei) /hej/, remember to make the breathy first sound. If you drop the pitch too soon, you sound bored instead of welcoming.
articles.summary: Learn how to pronounce short Romanian calls like hei with the right tone and pitch.

articles.title: Practice: Read Sentences in Chunks
articles.body:
## The sound
You group your words into chunks when you speak Romanian. A comma marks a pause between chunks. Your tone rises slightly at the comma. It shows that your thought is not finished yet. At the period, your pitch falls. This falling tone shows the end of the sentence.

## How to say it
Listen to (Mâine, merg la școală) /ˈmɨ.i.ne merɡ la ʃkoˈa.lə/. It means tomorrow I go to school. Raise your voice pitch slightly before the comma. Pause briefly at that mark. Then, say the second chunk and lower your tone.

## Reading rules
Every comma in a Romanian sentence creates a small border. You break long thoughts into easy parts at these marks. Never rush past a comma. Keep your voice tone high or level before the break. When you see a period, lower your tone firmly. The punctuation guides the music of your speech.

## Common mistakes
